entries.what: Robert Walton writes to his sister Mrs. Saville from St. Petersburg, assuring her of his welfare and confidence in his upcoming expedition.
entries.quote: TO Mrs. Saville, England / You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings.

entries.what: Walton feels a cold northern breeze in St. Petersburg that fills him with delight and braces his nerves, foretasting the icy climes he is advancing toward.
entries.quote: I am already far north of London, and as I walk in the streets of Petersburgh, I feel a cold northern breeze play upon my cheeks, which braces my nerves and fills me with delight.

entries.what: Walton imagines the North Pole as a region of beauty and perpetual sunlight, where snow and frost are banished and the sun is forever visible just skirting the horizon.
entries.quote: Inspirited by this wind of promise, my daydreams become more fervent and vivid. I try in vain to be persuaded that the pole is the seat of frost and desolation; it ever presents itself to my imagination as the region of beauty and delight.

entries.what: Walton has dedicated six years to his expedition and recalls the hour he committed himself to this great enterprise.
entries.when: Six years have passed since I resolved on my present undertaking.
entries.quote: Six years have passed since I resolved on my present undertaking. I can, even now, remember the hour from which I dedicated myself to this great enterprise.

entries.what: Walton endured hardship by accompanying whale-fishers to the North Sea, voluntarily enduring cold, famine, thirst, and want of sleep, and studied mathematics and physical science during nights.
entries.quote: I commenced by inuring my body to hardship. I accompanied the whale-fishers on several expeditions to the North Sea; I voluntarily endured cold, famine, thirst, and want of sleep; I often worked harder than the common sailors during the day and devoted my nights to the study of mathematics, the theory of medicine, and those branches of physical science from which a naval adventurer might derive the greatest practical advantage.

entries.what: Walton hired himself as an under-mate in a Greenland whaler and acquitted himself admirably, earning his captain's desire for him to remain.
entries.quote: Twice I actually hired myself as an under-mate in a Greenland whaler, and acquitted myself to admiration. I must own I felt a little proud when my captain offered me the second dignity in the vessel and entreated me to remain with the greatest earnestness.

entries.what: Walton plans to depart for Archangel in a fortnight or three weeks, hire a ship there, and engage sailors accustomed to whale-fishing, intending to sail in June.
entries.quote: I shall depart for the latter town in a fortnight or three weeks; and my intention is to hire a ship there, which can easily be done by paying the insurance for the owner, and to engage as many sailors as I think necessary among those who are accustomed to the whale-fishing. I do not intend to sail until the month of June.

entries.what: Walton expresses uncertainty about returning, stating that if he succeeds, many months or years may pass before he meets his sister again, but if he fails, she will see him soon or never.
entries.quote: If I succeed, many, many months, perhaps years, will pass before you and I may meet. If I fail, you will see me again soon, or never.

entries.what: Walton prefers glory over the ease and luxury his wealth could provide, and his courage and resolution are firm despite fluctuating hopes and depressed spirits.
entries.quote: My life might have been passed in ease and luxury, but I preferred glory to every enticement that wealth placed in my path. My courage and my resolution is firm; but my hopes fluctuate, and my spirits are often depressed.

entries.what: Walton requests his sister's leave to trust preceding navigators regarding the North Pole's wonders, believing he may discover a land surpassing every region hitherto discovered.
entries.quote: with your leave, my sister, I will put some trust in preceding navigators--there snow and frost are banished; and, sailing over a calm sea, we may be wafted to a land surpassing in wonders and in beauty every region hitherto discovered on the habitable globe.

entries.what: Robert Walton is writing a letter to his sister Mrs. Saville from Archangel, expressing his loneliness and desire for a friend during his dangerous expedition.
entries.why: Walton states he has no friend to share his joy or sustain him in disappointment, feeling the absence of companionship as a severe evil.
entries.quote: I have no friend, Margaret: when I am glowing with the enthusiasm of success, there will be none to participate my joy;

entries.what: Walton has hired a vessel and is collecting sailors for his expedition, having already engaged dependable and courageous men.
entries.why: Walton states he has hired a vessel and is occupied in collecting his sailors, who are men he can depend on and who are possessed of dauntless courage.
entries.quote: I have hired a vessel and am occupied in collecting my sailors; those whom I have already engaged appear to be men on whom I can depend and are certainly possessed of dauntless courage.

entries.what: Walton's lieutenant is a man of wonderful courage and enterprise, madly desirous of glory or advancement in his profession, and is an Englishman with noble endowments despite national and professional prejudices.
entries.why: Walton describes his lieutenant as a man of wonderful courage and enterprise, madly desirous of glory, or rather, of advancement in his profession.
entries.quote: My lieutenant, for instance, is a man of wonderful courage and enterprise; he is madly desirous of glory, or rather, to word my phrase more characteristically, of advancement in his profession.

entries.what: The master of the vessel is a person of excellent disposition, remarkable for his gentleness and mildness of discipline, with well-known integrity and dauntless courage.
entries.why: Walton describes the master as a person of an excellent disposition and is remarkable in the ship for his gentleness and the mildness of his discipline, with well-known integrity and dauntless courage.
entries.quote: The master is a person of an excellent disposition and is remarkable in the ship for his gentleness and the mildness of his discipline.

entries.what: Walton hired the master after hearing of his kindliness of heart and the respect and obedience paid to him by his crew, as Walton dislikes the usual brutality on board ship.
entries.why: Walton states he has never believed it necessary to exercise brutality on ship and felt particularly fortunate to secure the services of a mariner noted for kindliness of heart and respect from his crew.
entries.quote: I have never believed it to be necessary, and when I heard of a mariner equally noted for his kindliness of heart and the respect and obedience paid to him by his crew, I felt myself peculiarly fortunate in being able to secure his services.

entries.what: The master previously abandoned a romantic pursuit of a young Russian lady to allow her to marry another man she loved, giving her his money and soliciting her father's consent.
entries.why: The master loved a young Russian lady, but upon learning she loved another poor man, he instantly abandoned his pursuit, bestowed his money and farm on the rival, and solicited the father to consent to the union.
entries.quote: Some years ago he loved a young Russian lady of moderate fortune, and having amassed a considerable sum in prize-money, the father of the girl consented to the match. He saw his mistress once before the destined ceremony; but she was bathed in tears, and throwing herself at his feet, entreated him to spare her, confessing at the same time that she loved another, but that he was poor, and that her father would never consent to the union. My generous friend reassured the suppliant, and on being informed of the name of her lover, instantly abandoned his pursuit. He had already bought a farm with his money, on which he had designed to pass the remainder of his life; but he bestowed the whole on his rival, together with the remains of his prize-money to purchase stock, and then himself solicited the young woman's father to consent to her marriage with her lover.

entries.what: Walton is self-educated and feels illiterate compared to schoolboys, having run wild on a common and read only his uncle's books of voyages for the first fourteen years of his life.
entries.why: Walton states he is self-educated and that for the first fourteen years of his life he ran wild on a common and read nothing but his Uncle Thomas' books of voyages, making him more illiterate than many schoolboys of fifteen.
entries.quote: for the first fourteen years of my life I ran wild on a common and read nothing but our Uncle Thomas' books of voyages. At that age I became acquainted with the celebrated poets of our own country;

entries.what: Walton feels his daydreams lack keeping and greatly needs a friend to regulate his mind and not despise him as romantic.
entries.why: Walton states his daydreams want keeping and he greatly needs a friend who would have sense enough not to despise him as romantic, and affection enough to endeavour to regulate his mind.
entries.quote: I greatly need a friend who would have sense enough not to despise me as romantic, and affection enough for me to endeavour to regulate my mind.

entries.what: The winter has been dreadfully severe, but spring promises well and is considered a remarkably early season, possibly allowing Walton to sail sooner than expected.
entries.why: Walton notes the winter has been dreadfully severe, but the spring promises well and is considered a remarkably early season, so that he may sail sooner than expected.
entries.quote: The winter has been dreadfully severe, but the spring promises well, and it is considered as a remarkably early season, so that perhaps I may sail sooner than I expected.

entries.what: Walton is determined to proceed with his voyage and will not act rashly, relying on his prudence and considerateness regarding the safety of others.
entries.why: Walton states his resolutions are as fixed as fate and he will do nothing rashly, knowing the reader can confide in his prudence and considerateness when the safety of others is committed to his care.
entries.quote: Those are as fixed as fate, and my voyage is only now delayed until the weather shall permit my embarkation.

entries.what: Walton alludes to the Ancient Mariner, stating he will kill no albatross and fears he may return worn and woeful like that figure.
entries.why: Walton discloses he has often attributed his attachment to the dangerous mysteries of ocean to a poetic production, and assures his sister he will not kill an albatross.
entries.quote: I am going to unexplored regions, to 'the land of mist and snow,' but I shall kill no albatross; therefore do not be alarmed for my safety or if I should come back to you as worn and woeful as the 'Ancient Mariner.'

entries.what: Walton believes he has a love for the marvellous and a belief in the marvellous intertwined in all his projects, hurrying him out of common pathways to the wild sea and unvisited regions.
entries.why: Walton states there is a love for the marvellous, a belief in the marvellous, intertwined in all his projects, which hurries him out of the common pathways of men even to the wild sea and unvisited regions he is about to explore.
entries.quote: But besides this there is a love for the marvellous, a belief in the marvellous, intertwined in all my projects, which hurries me out of the common pathways of men, even to the wild sea and unvisited regions I am about to explore.

entries.what: Walton asks his sister to continue writing to him by every opportunity, as he may receive her letters on occasions when he needs them most to support his spirits.
entries.why: Walton requests his sister to continue writing to him by every opportunity, as he may receive her letters on some occasions when he needs them most to support his spirits.
entries.quote: Continue for the present to write to me by every opportunity: I may receive your letters on some occasions when I need them most to support my spirits.

entries.what: Walton loves his sister very tenderly and asks her to remember him with affection should she never hear from him again.
entries.why: Walton expresses his tender love for his sister and asks her to remember him with affection should she never hear from him again.
entries.quote: I love you very tenderly. Remember me with affection, should you never hear from me again.

entries.what: The writer is writing to his sister Mrs. Saville from a ship in the Arctic.
entries.quote: To Mrs. Saville, England / My dear Sister, / I write a few lines in haste to say that I am safe--and well advanced on my voyage.

entries.what: The writer is traveling north toward the Arctic and may not see his native land for many years.
entries.quote: This letter will reach England by a merchantman now on its homeward voyage from Archangel; more fortunate than I, who may not see my native land, perhaps, for many years.

entries.what: The writer's men are bold and firm of purpose despite the dangers of floating ice sheets.
entries.quote: my men are bold and apparently firm of purpose, nor do the floating sheets of ice that continually pass us, indicating the dangers of the region towards which we are advancing, appear to dismay them.

entries.what: The writer has reached a very high latitude during midsummer.
entries.quote: We have already reached a very high latitude; but it is the height of summer.

entries.what: The writer is determined to continue his voyage despite the risks.
entries.quote: Why not still proceed over the untamed yet obedient element? What can stop the determined heart and resolved will of man?

entries.what: The writer resolves to be cool, persevering, and prudent to avoid rash danger.
entries.quote: I will not rashly encounter danger. I will be cool, persevering, and prudent.

entries.what: The ship was nearly surrounded by ice on July 31st, trapping them with thick fog.
entries.why: Ice closed in the ship on all sides, scarcely leaving sea-room.
entries.quote: Last Monday (July 31st) we were nearly surrounded by ice, which closed in the ship on all sides, scarcely leaving her the sea-room in which she floated.

entries.what: A strange sight of a low carriage on a sledge drawn by dogs passed towards the north, carrying a gigantic man.
entries.when: About two o'clock after the fog cleared (July 31st)
entries.why: The mist cleared and they beheld vast plains of ice; the sight diverted their solicitude from their own situation.
entries.quote: We perceived a low carriage, fixed on a sledge and drawn by dogs, pass on towards the north, at the distance of half a mile; a being which had the shape of a man, but apparently of gigantic stature, sat in the sledge and guided the dogs.

entries.what: The sailors rescued a frozen, emaciated European man from a drifting sledge on ice two days later.
entries.when: About two hours after the ice broke and freed the ship, before night on July 31st
entries.why: Only one dog remained alive; a human being was within the sledge, and sailors persuaded him to enter the vessel.
entries.quote: It was, in fact, a sledge, like that we had seen before, which had drifted towards us in the night on a large fragment of ice. Only one dog remained alive; but there was a human being within it whom the sailors were persuading to enter the vessel.

entries.what: The rescued man was in a wretched condition with nearly frozen limbs and a body dreadfully emaciated by fatigue and suffering.
entries.when: Immediately after being rescued on July 31st
entries.why: He had been exposed to the cold and perilous situation on the ice.
entries.quote: His limbs were nearly frozen, and his body dreadfully emaciated by fatigue and suffering. I never saw a man in so wretched a condition.

entries.what: The stranger recovered slowly after being given brandy and soup, and showed moments of benevolence when kindness was shown.
entries.when: Two days passed after rescue before he could speak (August 1st-2nd)
entries.why: Slow degrees he recovered and ate a little soup, which restored him wonderfully.
entries.quote: As soon as he showed signs of life we wrapped him up in blankets and placed him near the chimney of the kitchen stove. By slow degrees he recovered and ate a little soup, which restored him wonderfully.

entries.what: The stranger became melancholy and despairing, sometimes gnashing his teeth from the weight of his woes, but lit up with benevolence at acts of kindness.
entries.why: His countenance generally had an expression of wildness and madness, but kindness lit it up with benevolence.
entries.quote: His eyes have generally an expression of wildness, and even madness, but there are moments when, if anyone performs an act of kindness towards him or does him any the most trifling service, his whole countenance is lighted up, as it were, with a beam of benevolence and sweetness that I never saw equalled.

entries.what: The stranger asked the lieutenant why he came so far upon the ice in so strange a vehicle, and replied he came to seek one who fled from him.
entries.when: After the lieutenant asked about his vehicle (August 1st-2nd)
entries.why: To seek one who fled from him; the man he pursued traveled in the same fashion.
entries.quote: Why he had come so far upon the ice in so strange a vehicle. His countenance instantly assumed an aspect of the deepest gloom, and he replied, 'To seek one who fled from me.'

entries.what: The stranger confirmed they had seen the other sledge the day before picking him up, and asked many questions about the route the 'demon' had pursued.
entries.why: He called the other man a demon and wanted to know the route he pursued.
entries.quote: Then I fancy we have seen him, for the day before we picked you up we saw some dogs drawing a sledge, with a man in it, across the ice.

entries.what: The stranger expressed eagerness to be on deck to watch for the sledge that preceded his own, but was persuaded to stay in the cabin due to weakness.
entries.why: He is far too weak to sustain the rawness of the atmosphere.
entries.quote: He manifested the greatest eagerness to be upon deck to watch for the sledge which had before appeared; but I have persuaded him to remain in the cabin, for he is far too weak to sustain the rawness of the atmosphere.

entries.what: The stranger revealed he had lost everything and could not begin life anew, contrasting with Walton's hope and the world before him.
entries.why: He once had a friend, the most noble of human creatures, and is entitled to judge respecting friendship; but he has lost everything.
entries.quote: I once had a friend, the most noble of human creatures, and am entitled, therefore, to judge respecting friendship. You have hope, and the world before you, and have no cause for despair. But I--I have lost everything and cannot begin life anew.

entries.what: The stranger possesses an intuitive discernment, a quick power of judgment, and a penetrating clarity into the causes of things, with a facility of expression and a voice like soul-subduing music.
entries.why: His mind is cultivated; when he speaks, words are culled with the choicest art yet flow with rapidity and unparalleled eloquence.
entries.quote: I believe it to be an intuitive discernment, a quick but never-failing power of judgment, a penetration into the causes of things, unequalled for clearness and precision; add to this a facility of expression and a voice whose varied intonations are soul-subduing music.

entries.what: The stranger began narrating his disastrous tale, hoping Walton may deduce a moral from his misfortunes to guide or console him.
entries.why: He seeks to relate occurrences usually deemed marvellous, hoping to impart internal evidence of truth and perhaps console Walton in case of failure.
entries.quote: You seek for knowledge and wisdom, as I once did; and I ardently hope that the gratification of your wishes may not be a serpent to sting you, as mine has been.

entries.what: The narrator is a Genevese by birth from a distinguished family, with ancestors who were counsellors and syndics.
entries.quote: I am by birth a Genevese, and my family is one of the most distinguished of that republic.

entries.what: The narrator's father held several public situations with honour and reputation and was respected for his integrity and attention to public business.
entries.quote: My father had filled several public situations with honour and reputation. He was respected by all who knew him for his integrity and indefatigable attention to public business.

entries.what: The narrator's father delayed marriage until later in life due to being occupied with country affairs.
entries.quote: He passed his younger days perpetually occupied by the affairs of his country; a variety of circumstances had prevented his marrying early, nor was it until the decline of life that he became a husband and the father of a family.

entries.what: Beaufort, a close friend of the narrator's father, fell into poverty and retreated to Lucerne with his daughter to live in obscurity and wretchedness.
entries.quote: One of his most intimate friends was a merchant who, from a flourishing state, fell, through numerous mischances, into poverty. This man, whose name was Beaufort, was of a proud and unbending disposition and could not bear to live in poverty and oblivion in the same country where he had formerly been distinguished for his rank and magnificence.

entries.what: The narrator's father searched for Beaufort for ten months to persuade him to begin the world again with his credit and assistance.
entries.quote: He lost no time in endeavouring to seek him out, with the hope of persuading him to begin the world again through his credit and assistance. Beaufort had taken effectual measures to conceal himself, and it was ten months before my father discovered his abode.

entries.what: Beaufort had saved a small sum of money from his ruined fortune, which was sufficient for sustenance for some months while he hoped to find respectable employment.
entries.quote: Beaufort had saved but a very small sum of money from the wreck of his fortunes, but it was sufficient to provide him with sustenance for some months, and in the meantime he hoped to procure some respectable employment in a merchant's house.

entries.what: Beaufort fell ill and became incapable of exertion after three months of grief and reflection following his poverty.
entries.quote: his grief only became more deep and rankling when he had leisure for reflection, and at length it took so fast hold of his mind that at the end of three months he lay on a bed of sickness, incapable of any exertion.

entries.what: Caroline Beaufort, Beaufort's daughter, showed uncommon courage and industriousness by plaiting straw and doing plain work to earn money for support.
entries.quote: She procured plain work; she plaited straw and by various means contrived to earn a pittance scarcely sufficient to support life.

entries.what: Beaufort died in the tenth month after falling into poverty, leaving Caroline an orphan and a beggar.
entries.quote: Several months passed in this manner. Her father grew worse; her time was more entirely occupied in attending him; her means of subsistence decreased; and in the tenth month her father died in her arms, leaving her an orphan and a beggar.

entries.what: The narrator's father found Caroline weeping by Beaufort's coffin and took her under his protection, later conducting her to Geneva and placing her under the protection of a relation.
entries.quote: He came like a protecting spirit to the poor girl, who committed herself to his care; and after the interment of his friend he conducted her to Geneva and placed her under the protection of a relation.

entries.what: There was a considerable age difference between the narrator's parents, but it brought them closer in devoted affection.
entries.quote: There was a considerable difference between the ages of my parents, but this circumstance seemed to unite them only closer in bonds of devoted affection.

entries.what: The narrator's father loved the mother with reverence for her virtues and a desire to recompensate her for her sorrows, differing from mere doting fondness of age.
entries.quote: There was a show of gratitude and worship in his attachment to my mother, differing wholly from the doting fondness of age, for it was inspired by reverence for her virtues and a desire to be the means of, in some degree, recompensing her for the sorrows she had endured.

entries.what: The narrator's father sought to shelter the mother like a fair exotic, surrounding her with all that could excite pleasurable emotion and protect her from rougher winds.
entries.quote: He strove to shelter her, as a fair exotic is sheltered by the gardener, from every rougher wind and to surround her with all that could tend to excite pleasurable emotion in her soft and benevolent mind.

entries.what: The narrator's parents traveled to Italy after their marriage as a restorative for the mother's weakened frame from her past sorrows.
entries.quote: immediately after their union they sought the pleasant climate of Italy, and the change of scene and interest attendant on a tour through that land of wonders, as a restorative for her weakened frame.

entries.what: The narrator was born at Naples and as an infant accompanied his parents on their travels.
entries.quote: I, their eldest child, was born at Naples, and as an infant accompanied them in their rambles.

entries.what: The narrator was an only child for several years, the beloved plaything and idol of his parents who directed his future toward happiness or misery.
entries.quote: I remained for several years their only child. Much as they were attached to each other, they seemed to draw inexhaustible stores of affection from a very mine of love to bestow them upon me.

entries.what: The narrator's mother had a benevolent disposition and a passion for relieving the afflicted, remembering her own past suffering and relief.
entries.quote: Their benevolent disposition often made them enter the cottages of the poor. This, to my mother, was more than a duty; it was a necessity, a passion--remembering what she had suffered, and how she had been relieved--for her to act in her turn the guardian angel to the afflicted.

entries.what: While traveling in Italy, the narrator's mother encountered a poor cottage with hungry children, including a fair-haired girl who stood out as distinct and heaven-sent.
entries.quote: During one of their walks a poor cot in the foldings of a vale attracted their notice as being singularly disconsolate, while the number of half-clothed children gathered about it spoke of penury in its worst shape.

entries.what: The fair-haired girl, Elizabeth Lavenza, was the daughter of a Milanese nobleman whose property was confiscated and who became a victim of Austria, leaving her an orphan and beggar.
entries.quote: She was not her child, but the daughter of a Milanese nobleman. Her mother was a German and had died on giving her birth. The infant had been placed with these good people to nurse: they were better off then.

entries.what: The narrator's mother prevailed upon the peasant guardians to yield charge of Elizabeth, who became the inmate of the parents' house as 'my more than sister' and 'the beautiful and adored companion of all my occupations and my pleasures.'
entries.quote: With his permission my mother prevailed on her rustic guardians to yield their charge to her. They were fond of the sweet orphan. Her presence had seemed a blessing to them, but it would be unfair to her to keep her in poverty and want when Providence afforded her such powerful protection.

entries.what: Everyone loved Elizabeth, and the narrator regarded her as his own to protect, love, and cherish, interpreting his mother's gift literally as a present for him.
entries.quote: On the evening previous to her being brought to my home, my mother had said playfully, 'I have a pretty present for my Victor--tomorrow he shall have it.' And when, on the morrow, she presented Elizabeth to me as her promised gift, I, with childish seriousness, interpreted her words literally and looked upon Elizabeth as mine--mine to protect, love, and cherish.

entries.what: The narrator and Elizabeth called each other cousin, but the narrator considered her his more than sister, since till death she was to be mine only.
entries.quote: We called each other familiarly by the name of cousin. No word, no expression could body forth the kind of relation in which she stood to me--my more than sister, since till death she was to be mine only.

entries.what: Victor and Elizabeth were raised together from childhood with a close, harmonious relationship, differing in temperament but drawn together by their contrasting natures.
entries.quote: We were brought up together; there was not quite a year difference in our ages. Harmony was the soul of our companionship...

entries.what: Victor's father dismisses Cornelius Agrippa as 'sad trash' without explaining its content, causing Victor to become more determined to read it.
entries.quote: My father looked carelessly at the title page of my book and said, 'Ah! Cornelius Agrippa! My dear Victor, do not waste your time upon this; it is sad trash.'

entries.what: Victor becomes deeply engrossed in reading the works of Agrippa, Paracelsus, and Albertus Magnus, finding them full of 'wild fancies' and 'treasures known to few besides myself.'
entries.quote: I continued to read with the greatest avidity. When I returned home my first care was to procure the whole works of this author, and afterwards of Paracelsus and Albertus Magnus.

entries.what: Victor is fascinated by the philosopher's stone and the elixir of life, desiring to banish disease and render man invulnerable to violent death.
entries.quote: Under the guidance of my new preceptors I entered with the greatest diligence into the search of the philosopher's stone and the elixir of life; but the latter soon obtained my undivided attention.

entries.what: Victor witnesses a violent thunderstorm where an oak tree is struck by lightning and shattered into thin ribbons, fascinating him with the power of electricity.
entries.quote: I remained, while the storm lasted, watching its progress with curiosity and delight. As I stood at the door, on a sudden I beheld a stream of fire issue from an old and beautiful oak...

entries.what: A natural philosopher explains to Victor a new theory of electricity and galvanism that supersedes the ancient authors he previously admired, causing him to temporarily abandon those studies.
entries.quote: All that he said threw greatly into the shade Cornelius Agrippa, Albertus Magnus, and Paracelsus, the lords of my imagination; but by some fatality the overthrow of these men disinclined me to pursue my accustomed studies.

entries.what: Victor abruptly gives up his study of Agrippa and the ancient alchemists, turning instead to mathematics, which he sees as having 'secure foundations.'
entries.quote: I at once gave up my former occupations, set down natural history and all its progeny as a deformed and abortive creation, and entertained the greatest disdain for a would-be science which could never even step within the threshold of real knowledge.

entries.what: Victor reflects that his sudden shift in interests was likely the 'last effort made by the spirit of preservation' to avert his future destruction, associating evil with the pursuit of knowledge.
entries.quote: When I look back, it seems to me as if this almost miraculous change of inclination and will was the immediate suggestion of the guardian angel of my life--the last effort made by the spirit of preservation to avert the storm that was even then hanging in the stars...

entries.what: Victor becomes obsessed with natural philosophy and chemistry, making it his sole occupation.
entries.quote: From this day natural philosophy, and particularly chemistry, in the most comprehensive sense of the term, became nearly my sole occupation.

entries.what: Victor attends lectures and cultivates acquaintance with university men of science, including M. Krempe and M. Waldman.
entries.quote: I attended the lectures and cultivated the acquaintance of the men of science of the university, and I found even in M. Krempe a great deal of sound sense and real information...

entries.what: Victor makes rapid progress in chemistry, astonishing students and masters alike.
entries.quote: My application was at first fluctuating and uncertain; it gained strength as I proceeded and soon became so ardent and eager that the stars often disappeared in the light of morning whilst I was yet engaged in my laboratory.

entries.what: Two years pass during which Victor remains in Ingolstadt and does not visit Geneva.
entries.quote: Two years passed in this manner, during which I paid no visit to Geneva, but was engaged, heart and soul, in the pursuit of some discoveries which I hoped to make.

entries.what: Victor becomes fascinated with the structure of the human frame and the origin of life.
entries.quote: One of the phenomena which had peculiarly attracted my attention was the structure of the human frame, and, indeed, any animal endued with life. Whence, I often asked myself, did the principle of life proceed?

entries.what: Victor determines to apply himself to natural philosophy relating to physiology.
entries.quote: I revolved these circumstances in my mind and determined thenceforth to apply myself more particularly to those branches of natural philosophy which relate to physiology.

entries.what: Victor studies anatomy and the decay of the human body, spending days and nights in vaults and charnel-houses.
entries.quote: I became acquainted with the science of anatomy, but this was not sufficient; I must also observe the natural decay and corruption of the human body. I saw how the fine form of man was degraded and wasted...

entries.what: Victor discovers the cause of generation and life, becoming capable of bestowing animation on lifeless matter.
entries.quote: After days and nights of incredible labour and fatigue, I succeeded in discovering the cause of generation and life; nay, more, I became myself capable of bestowing animation upon lifeless matter.

entries.what: Victor feels delight and rapture at his discovery, considering it the summit of his desires.
entries.quote: The astonishment which I had at first experienced on this discovery soon gave place to delight and rapture. After so much time spent in painful labour, to arrive at once at the summit of my desires was the most gratifying consummation of my toils.

entries.what: Victor hesitates on how to employ his power to bestow animation, debating creating a being like himself or simpler.
entries.quote: When I found so astonishing a power placed within my hands, I hesitated a long time concerning the manner in which I should employ it.

entries.what: Victor decides to create a being of gigantic stature, about eight feet tall, due to the minuteness of parts hindering his speed.
entries.quote: I resolved, contrary to my first intention, to make the being of a gigantic stature, that is to say, about eight feet in height, and proportionably large.

entries.what: Victor works unremittingly on his creation, neglecting health and friends, while the seasons pass.
entries.quote: The summer months passed while I was thus engaged, heart and soul, in one pursuit. It was a most beautiful season; never did the fields bestow a more plentiful harvest or the vines yield a more luxuriant vintage, but my eyes were insensible to the charms of nature.

entries.what: Victor's physical and mental health deteriorates as he nears completion of his creation.
entries.quote: My cheek had grown pale with study, and my person had become emaciated with confinement. Sometimes, on the very brink of certainty, I failed; yet still I clung to the hope which the next day or the next hour might realize.

entries.what: Victor reflects that the pursuit of knowledge can weaken affections and destroy taste for simple pleasures, making it unlawful if it disturbs domestic tranquillity.
entries.quote: If the study to which you apply yourself has a tendency to weaken your affections and to destroy your taste for those simple pleasures in which no alloy can possibly mix, then that study is certainly unlawful, that is to say, not befitting the human mind.

entries.what: Elizabeth writes to Victor expressing concern about his illness and asking him to write to reassure her, mentioning that his father longs to see him and that Ernest has improved.
entries.why: Elizabeth is anxious about Victor's health and wants confirmation of his recovery.
entries.quote: You are forbidden to write--to hold a pen; yet one word from you, dear Victor, is necessary to calm our apprehensions.

entries.what: Elizabeth describes the peaceful and unchanged natural scenery of Geneva, including the blue lake and snow-clad mountains, and reflects on the contented hearts of the family.
entries.why: Elizabeth describes the setting and family state in her letter to Victor.
entries.quote: The blue lake and snow-clad mountains--they never change; and I think our placid home and our contented hearts are regulated by the same immutable laws.

entries.what: Elizabeth relates the history of Justine Moritz, who came to live with the family after her mother could not endure her, and was educated by Victor's aunt.
entries.why: Elizabeth provides Justine's backstory in her letter to Victor.
entries.quote: Madame Moritz, her mother, was a widow with four children, of whom Justine was the third. This girl had always been the favourite of her father, but through a strange perversity, her mother could not endure her...

entries.what: Elizabeth describes William Frankenstein as very tall for his age with sweet laughing blue eyes, dark eyelashes, and curling hair, noting dimples when he smiles.
entries.why: Elizabeth describes William's appearance in her letter to Victor.
entries.quote: He is very tall of his age, with sweet laughing blue eyes, dark eyelashes, and curling hair. When he smiles, two little dimples appear on each cheek, which are rosy with health.

entries.what: Victor feels a violent antipathy to the name of natural philosophy after his creation, and the sight of chemical instruments renews his agony.
entries.why: Victor has conceived a violent antipathy to natural philosophy since the fatal night and the beginning of his misfortunes.
entries.quote: Ever since the fatal night, the end of my labours, and the beginning of my misfortunes, I had conceived a violent antipathy even to the name of natural philosophy.

entries.what: Professor M. Waldman praises Victor's progress in the sciences, not knowing it causes Victor pain, and changes the subject to the science itself to draw him out.
entries.why: M. Waldman wants to please Victor and draw him into conversation about science.
entries.quote: He soon perceived that I disliked the subject; but not guessing the real cause, he attributed my feelings to modesty, and changed the subject from my improvement, to the science itself...

entries.what: Professor M. Krempe harshly praises Victor, saying he has outstript them all, and makes a blunt comment about young men being diffident.
entries.why: M. Krempe commends Victor's progress in a harsh manner, not realizing Victor's suffering.
entries.quote: D--n the fellow! why, M. Clerval, I assure you he has outstript us all. Ay, stare if you please; but it is nevertheless true.

entries.what: Clerval has different literary pursuits than Victor, focusing on oriental languages such as Persian, Arabic, and Sanskrit, and encourages Victor to join him.
entries.why: Clerval came to the university to master oriental languages and open a field for his life plan, and induced Victor to enter the same studies.
entries.quote: Clerval had never sympathized in my tastes for natural science; and his literary pursuits differed wholly from those which had occupied me. He came to the university with the design of making himself complete master of the oriental languages...

entries.what: Victor and Clerval take a pedestrian tour in the environs of Ingolstadt, enjoying nature and each other's company, which restores Victor's spirits.
entries.why: Henry proposed a pedestrian tour so Victor could bid a personal farewell to the country he had long inhabited.
entries.quote: We passed a fortnight in these perambulations: my health and spirits had long been restored, and they gained additional strength from the salubrious air I breathed, the natural incidents of our progress, and the conversation of my friend.

entries.what: Victor's journey to Geneva is delayed by winter snow and impassable roads, and he waits until spring to travel, reluctant to leave Clerval.
entries.why: Victor's return was delayed from an unwillingness to leave Clerval in a strange place before he had become acquainted with its inhabitants, and winter snow made roads impassable.
entries.quote: My return had only been delayed so long, from an unwillingness to leave Clerval in a strange place, before he had become acquainted with any of its inhabitants. The winter, however, was spent cheerfully...

entries.what: Victor's parents decide he should attend the university of Ingolstadt at age seventeen.
entries.when: when Victor had attained the age of seventeen
entries.why: my father thought it necessary for the completion of my education that I should be made acquainted with other customs than those of my native country
entries.quote: When I had attained the age of seventeen my parents resolved that I should become a student at the university of Ingolstadt.

entries.what: Elizabeth contracts scarlet fever, nearly dying, and Victor's mother nurses her back to health.
entries.when: before the day resolved upon could arrive, the first misfortune of my life occurred--an omen, as it were, of my future misery. Elizabeth had caught the scarlet fever; her illness was severe, and she was in the greatest danger.
entries.why: Elizabeth had caught the scarlet fever; her illness was severe, and she was in the greatest danger.
entries.quote: Elizabeth had caught the scarlet fever; her illness was severe, and she was in the greatest danger.

entries.what: Victor's mother falls ill and dies after nursing Elizabeth, joining hands with Victor and Elizabeth on her deathbed.
entries.when: On the third day my mother sickened; her fever was accompanied by the most alarming symptoms, and the looks of her medical attendants prognosticated the worst event.
entries.why: the consequences of this imprudence were fatal to her preserver.
entries.quote: On her deathbed the fortitude and benignity of this best of women did not desert her. She joined the hands of Elizabeth and myself.

entries.what: Victor delays his departure for Ingolstadt out of grief and reluctance to leave his family, especially Elizabeth.
entries.when: My departure for Ingolstadt, which had been deferred by these events, was now again determined upon. I obtained from my father a respite of some weeks.
entries.why: I was unwilling to quit the sight of those that remained to me, and above all, I desired to see my sweet Elizabeth in some degree consoled.
entries.quote: I was unwilling to quit the sight of those that remained to me, and above all, I desired to see my sweet Elizabeth in some degree consoled.

entries.what: Henry Clerval wishes to accompany Victor to Ingolstadt but is forbidden by his father, who values commerce over liberal education.
entries.when: The day of my departure at length arrived. Clerval spent the last evening with us. He had endeavoured to persuade his father to permit him to accompany me and to become my fellow student, but in vain.
entries.why: His father was a narrow-minded trader and saw idleness and ruin in the aspirations and ambition of his son.
entries.quote: He had endeavoured to persuade his father to permit him to accompany me and to become my fellow student, but in vain. His father was a narrow-minded trader and saw idleness and ruin in the aspirations and ambition of his son.

entries.what: Victor arrives at Ingolstadt and is introduced to Professor Krempe, who dismisses his alchemical studies as useless nonsense.
entries.when: the next morning I delivered my letters of introduction and paid a visit to some of the principal professors. Chance--or rather the evil influence, the Angel of Destruction, which asserted omnipotent sway over me from the moment I turned my reluctant steps from my father's door--led me first to M. Krempe, professor of natural philosophy.
entries.why: Every minute, every instant that you have wasted on those books is utterly and entirely lost. You have burdened your memory with exploded systems and useless names.
entries.quote: Have you,

entries.what: Victor attends Professor Waldman's chemistry lecture and is inspired by his modern views, deciding to pursue science with renewed purpose.
entries.when: I went into the lecturing room, which M. Waldman entered shortly after. This professor was very unlike his colleague. He appeared about fifty years of age, but with an aspect expressive of the greatest benevolence.
entries.why: The modern masters promise very little; they know that metals cannot be transmuted and that the elixir of life is a chimera but these philosophers, whose hands seem only made to dabble in dirt, and their eyes to pore over the microscope or crucible, have indeed performed miracles.
entries.quote: The ancient teachers of this science, promised impossibilities and performed nothing. The modern masters promise very little; they know that metals cannot be transmuted and that the elixir of life is a chimera but these philosophers, whose hands seem only made to dabble in dirt, and their eyes to pore over the microscope or crucible, have indeed performed miracles.

entries.what: Victor creates the Creature on a dreary November night, bringing it to life with a spark.
entries.when: one in the morning of a dreary night of November
entries.why: Victor had long desired it with an ardour that far exceeded moderation, seeking to infuse life into an inanimate body.
entries.quote: It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils.

entries.what: The Creature has watery eyes, yellow skin, lustrous black hair, pearly white teeth, shriveled complexion, and straight black lips.
entries.when: immediately after the Creature opens its eyes
entries.why: Victor describes the Creature's physical features as he beholds it for the first time.
entries.quote: His yellow skin scarcely covered the work of muscles and arteries beneath; his hair was of a lustrous black, and flowing; his teeth of a pearly whiteness; but these luxuriances only formed a more horrid contrast with his watery eyes.

entries.what: Victor feels breathless horror and disgust upon seeing the Creature alive, despite his earlier efforts to make it beautiful.
entries.why: The beauty of the dream vanished, replaced by horror and disgust at the Creature's appearance.
entries.quote: But now that I had finished, the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart.

entries.what: Victor flees his room and spends the night walking the courtyard in agitation, fearing the Creature.
entries.when: the rest of the night after the Creature awakens
entries.why: Unable to endure the aspect of the being I had created, I rushed out of the room.
entries.quote: I rushed out of the room and continued a long time traversing my bed-chamber, unable to compose my mind to sleep.

entries.what: Victor dreams of Elizabeth turning into his dead mother, causing him to wake in horror.
entries.when: during the night after creating the Creature
entries.why: The different accidents of life are not so changeable as the feelings of human nature; his thoughts returned to Elizabeth and his mother.
entries.quote: I thought I saw Elizabeth, in the bloom of health, walking in the streets of Ingolstadt... her features appeared to change, and I thought that I held the corpse of my dead mother in my arms.

entries.what: The Creature stands at the bedside and watches Victor while he sleeps.
entries.when: the night after the Creature awakens
entries.why: The Creature had followed Victor from his room and stood by the bed.
entries.quote: He held up the curtain of the bed; and his eyes, if eyes they may be called, were fixed on me.

entries.what: Victor falls into a nervous fever and is confined to his room for several months.
entries.when: after the events of the night the Creature was created
entries.why: This was the commencement of a nervous fever which confined me for several months; his health broke down from the horror.
entries.quote: This was the commencement of a nervous fever which confined me for several months.

entries.what: Henry Clerval arrives in Ingolstadt and nurses Victor back to health.
entries.when: after Victor's fever begins; Henry had come to Ingolstadt to study
entries.why: Henry had come to Ingolstadt; knowing my father's advanced age and unfitness for so long a journey, and how wretched my sickness would make Elizabeth, he spared them this grief by concealing the extent of my disorder.
entries.quote: My dear Frankenstein,

entries.what: Victor fears the Creature will enter his room and reacts with terror when he sees a shadow.
entries.when: the morning after the Creature awakens; when he returns to his room
entries.why: I dreaded to behold this monster, but I feared still more that Henry should see him.
entries.quote: I threw the door forcibly open... but nothing appeared.

entries.what: Victor sees the Creature's shadow enter the room and has a fit; Clerval calls for help.
entries.when: the morning after Victor returns to his room
entries.why: I imagined that the monster seized me; I struggled furiously and fell down in a fit.
entries.quote: HE can tell. Oh, save me! Save me!

entries.what: Victor recovers from fever in spring, feeling joy as nature revives around him.
entries.when: springtime after several months of illness
entries.why: I remember the first time I became capable of observing outward objects with any kind of pleasure... It was a divine spring, and the season contributed greatly to my convalescence.
entries.quote: I remember the first time I became capable of observing outward objects with any kind of pleasure, I perceived that the fallen leaves had disappeared and that the young buds were shooting forth from the trees that shaded my window.

entries.what: William Frankenstein is murdered, his body found with finger marks on his neck.
entries.why: The text does not give a reason for the murder; it only describes the discovery of the body.
entries.quote: About five in the morning I discovered my lovely boy, whom the night before I had seen blooming and active in health, stretched on the grass livid and motionless; the print of the murder's finger was on his neck.

entries.what: Elizabeth feels guilty about William's death because he wore her miniature portrait.
entries.why: Elizabeth confesses she let William wear the valuable miniature of Victor's mother, which was later found on Justine.
entries.quote: She told me, that that same evening William had teased her to let him wear a very valuable miniature that she possessed of your mother. This picture is gone, and was doubtless the temptation which urged the murderer to the deed.

entries.what: Justine Moritz is accused and on trial for William's murder.
entries.when: The trial is set for the day after Victor arrives in Geneva
entries.why: The servant found the miniature in Justine's pocket, and her confused behavior added to the evidence against her.
entries.quote: No one did at first; but several circumstances came out, that have almost forced conviction upon us; and her own behaviour has been so confused, as to add to the evidence of facts a weight that, I fear, leaves no hope for doubt. But she will be tried today, and you will then hear all.

entries.what: Victor sees the creature near the murder scene and is convinced it killed William.
entries.when: The night of Victor's arrival near Geneva, after the storm
entries.why: Victor recognizes the creature's gigantic stature and deformity by lightning; the creature flees toward Mont Saleve.
entries.quote: A flash of lightning illuminated the object, and discovered its shape plainly to me; its gigantic stature, and the deformity of its aspect more hideous than belongs to humanity, instantly informed me that it was the wretch, the filthy daemon, to whom I had given life.

entries.what: Victor resolves to stay silent about the creature being the murderer.
entries.when: Upon entering his father's house in Geneva
entries.why: Victor fears no one would believe his story; he doubts he could pursue the creature, and worries it would be seen as madness.
entries.quote: I well knew that if any other had communicated such a relation to me, I should have looked upon it as the ravings of insanity. Besides, the strange nature of the animal would elude all pursuit.

entries.what: Victor travels to Geneva after receiving the letter about William's death.
entries.when: Chapter 7; journey takes several days, with a stop at Lausanne
entries.why: Victor's father urges him to return to console Elizabeth and the family.
entries.quote: To go instantly to Geneva: come with me, Henry, to order the horses.

entries.what: Victor views the countryside and reflects on his past happiness while traveling to Geneva.
entries.when: During the journey, passing through Lausanne and near Geneva
entries.why: The calm scenery temporarily restores Victor's spirits before grief returns.
entries.quote: I contemplated the lake: the waters were placid; all around was calm; and the snowy mountains, 'the palaces of nature,' were not changed. By degrees the calm and heavenly scene restored me.

entries.what: Victor arrives at Geneva at night and stays at Secheron, a village half a league away.
entries.why: The town gates were shut, forcing Victor to stay outside the city.
entries.quote: Completely dark when I arrived in the environs of Geneva; the gates of the town were already shut; and I was obliged to pass the night at Secheron, a village at the distance of half a league from the city.

entries.what: Elizabeth believes Justine is innocent and relies on her innocence.
entries.why: Elizabeth loves Justine and fears she will be condemned; she looks to Victor to prove Justine's innocence.
entries.quote: She welcomed me with the greatest affection. 'Your arrival, my dear cousin,' said she, 'fills me with hope. You perhaps will find some means to justify my poor guiltless Justine.'

entries.what: Victor's father hopes Justine will be acquitted at her trial.
entries.why: The father wants to prevent any partiality in the legal process.
entries.quote: If she is, as you believe, innocent, rely on the justice of our laws, and the activity with which I shall prevent the slightest shadow of partiality.

entries.what: Victor accompanies his family to the court for Justine's trial as a witness.
entries.why: My father and the rest of the family being obliged to attend as witnesses
entries.quote: We passed a few sad hours until eleven o'clock, when the trial was to commence. My father and the rest of the family being obliged to attend as witnesses, I accompanied them to the court.

entries.what: Justine is accused of murdering William Frankenstein, Victor's younger brother.
entries.why: the result of my curiosity and lawless devices would cause the death of two of my fellow beings: one a smiling babe full of innocence and joy, the other far more dreadfully murdered
entries.quote: It was to be decided whether the result of my curiosity and lawless devices would cause the death of two of my fellow beings: one a smiling babe full of innocence and joy, the other far more dreadfully murdered, with every aggravation of infamy that could make the murder memorable in horror.

entries.what: Justine was out the entire night of the murder and was found near the crime scene towards morning.
entries.why: She had been out the whole of the night on which the murder had been committed and towards morning had been perceived by a market-woman not far from the spot where the body of the murdered child had been afterwards found.
entries.quote: She had been out the whole of the night on which the murder had been committed and towards morning had been perceived by a market-woman not far from the spot where the body of the murdered child had been afterwards found.

entries.what: Justine claimed she spent the evening before the murder at her aunt's house in Chene and looked for the child after meeting a man who asked about him.
entries.why: by the permission of Elizabeth, she had passed the evening of the night on which the murder had been committed at the house of an aunt at Chene... On her return, at about nine o'clock, she met a man who asked her if she had seen anything of the child who was lost.
entries.quote: by the permission of Elizabeth, she had passed the evening of the night on which the murder had been committed at the house of an aunt at Chene, a village situated at about a league from Geneva. On her return, at about nine o'clock, she met a man who asked her if she had seen anything of the child who was lost.

entries.what: Elizabeth testifies to Justine's excellent character and expresses belief in her innocence.
entries.why: I am well acquainted with the accused. I have lived in the same house with her, at one time for five and at another for nearly two years. During all that period she appeared to me the most amiable and benevolent of human creatures.
entries.quote: I am well acquainted with the accused. I have lived in the same house with her, at one time for five and at another for nearly two years. During all that period she appeared to me the most amiable and benevolent of human creatures.

entries.what: Justine confesses to the crime, but later claims it was a false confession made to obtain absolution under pressure from her confessor.
entries.when: during the trial and after in Chapter 8
entries.why: I confessed, that I might obtain absolution; but now that falsehood lies heavier at my heart than all my other sins.
entries.quote: I did confess, but I confessed a lie. I confessed, that I might obtain absolution; but now that falsehood lies heavier at my heart than all my other sins.

entries.what: The court condemns Justine to death despite Elizabeth's passionate appeal and the jury seeing ballots all black.
entries.when: the morning after the trial in Chapter 8
entries.why: the ballots had been thrown; they were all black, and Justine was condemned.
entries.quote: the ballots had been thrown; they were all black, and Justine was condemned.

entries.what: Victor flees the court in agony upon hearing Justine's condemnation, believing himself the true murderer.
entries.why: I could not sustain the horror of my situation, and when I perceived that the popular voice and the countenances of the judges had already condemned my unhappy victim, I rushed out of the court in agony.
entries.quote: I could not sustain the horror of my situation, and when I perceived that the popular voice and the countenances of the judges had already condemned my unhappy victim, I rushed out of the court in agony.

entries.what: Victor visits Justine in prison and feels intense remorse, knowing he is the true murderer.
entries.when: after the trial and before Justine's execution in Chapter 8
entries.why: I gnashed my teeth and ground them together, uttering a groan that came from my inmost soul.
entries.quote: I gnashed my teeth and ground them together, uttering a groan that came from my inmost soul.

entries.what: Justine is executed on the scaffold the morning after the trial.
entries.when: the morrow after the trial in Chapter 8
entries.why: Elizabeth's heart-rending eloquence failed to move the judges from their settled conviction in the criminality of the saintly sufferer.
entries.quote: And on the morrow Justine died.

entries.what: Justine Moritz is executed, and Victor feels overwhelming guilt and despair, believing he is the true murderer.
entries.when: after Justine's death and before Victor's departure to the Alps
entries.why: Victor believes he created the monster that killed William and Justine; the text states he is 'the true murderer' in effect.
entries.quote: I was alive. The blood flowed freely in my veins, but a weight of despair and remorse pressed on my heart which nothing could remove.

entries.what: Victor's father advises him to control his grief to avoid adding to the family's unhappiness and to fulfill his duty to the survivors.
entries.when: during Victor's mourning period in Geneva
entries.why: The father argues that excessive sorrow prevents improvement, enjoyment, and daily usefulness, which is needed for society.
entries.quote: "Do you think, Victor, that I do not suffer also?... It is also a duty owed to yourself, for excessive sorrow prevents improvement or enjoyment..."

entries.what: Victor flees to the lake near Geneva at night to find temporary solace in solitude and the water.
entries.when: after the family moves to Belrive; often after the family has retired for the night
entries.why: The shutting of gates at ten o'clock made staying in Geneva irksome; Victor sought freedom on the lake.
entries.quote: Often, after the rest of the family had retired for the night, I took the boat and passed many hours upon the water.

entries.what: Victor contemplates drowning himself in the lake but is restrained by thoughts of Elizabeth, his father, and brother.
entries.when: while alone on the lake at night
entries.why: He thinks of Elizabeth, whom he loves, and fears leaving his father and brother exposed to the monster's malice.
entries.quote: But I was restrained, when I thought of the heroic and suffering Elizabeth, whom I tenderly loved, and whose existence was bound up in mine.

entries.what: The family is in a state of mourning; Elizabeth believes she is walking on the edge of a precipice and fears for her own happiness.
entries.why: Elizabeth laments the death of Justine and feels eternal woe and tears are the just tribute to innocence destroyed.
entries.quote: When I reflect, my dear cousin, on the miserable death of Justine Moritz, I no longer see the world and its works as they before appeared to me.

entries.what: Victor travels to the Alpine valleys, specifically the valley of Chamounix, to seek relief from his despair through nature's magnificence.
entries.when: about the middle of August, nearly two months after Justine's death
entries.why: Victor seeks to forget himself and his ephemeral human sorrows in the magnificence and eternity of the mountain scenes.
entries.quote: I suddenly left my home, and bending my steps towards the near Alpine valleys, sought in the magnificence, the eternity of such scenes, to forget myself and my ephemeral, because human, sorrows.

entries.what: Victor finds temporary solace in the sublime nature of the Alps, particularly Mont Blanc, which makes him cease to fear lesser beings.
entries.when: during his journey to Chamounix, ascending the valley of Arve
entries.why: The immense mountains, precipices, and the sound of the river and waterfalls spoke of a power mighty as Omnipotence, causing Victor to cease fearing lesser beings.
entries.quote: The immense mountains and precipices that overhung me on every side, the sound of the river raging among the rocks, and the dashing of the waterfalls around spoke of a power mighty as Omnipotence--and I ceased to fear or to bend before any being less almighty than that which had created and ruled the elements.

entries.what: Victor experiences a mix of pleasure and despair when reminded of his boyhood while traveling through the Alps.
entries.when: during his journey to Chamounix, noticing new objects and turns in the road
entries.why: Some turn in the road or new object reminded him of days gone by and were associated with the lighthearted gaiety of boyhood, but the kindly influence ceased, and he fell back into misery.
entries.quote: Some turn in the road, some new object suddenly perceived and recognized, reminded me of days gone by, and were associated with the lighthearted gaiety of boyhood.

entries.what: Victor arrives at the village of Chamounix and falls asleep to the sounds of Mont Blanc and the Arve river, finding oblivion.
entries.when: at length I arrived at the village of Chamounix
entries.why: Exhaustion succeeded to the extreme fatigue of body and mind; the lulling sounds of nature acted as a lullaby, and sleep crept over him.
entries.quote: For a short space of time I remained at the window watching the pallid lightnings that played above Mont Blanc and listening to the rushing of the Arve, which pursued its noisy way beneath. The same lulling sounds acted as a lullaby to my too keen sensations; when I placed my head upon my pillow, sleep crept over me.

entries.what: The narrator roamed the valley and stood beside the sources of the Arveiron, which rise from a glacier advancing down from the hills.
entries.quote: I stood beside the sources of the Arveiron, which take their rise in a glacier, that with slow pace is advancing down from the summit of the hills to barricade the valley.

entries.what: The narrator found consolation in the sublime and magnificent natural scenes, which elevated him above littleness of feeling and tranquillized his grief.
entries.quote: These sublime and magnificent scenes afforded me the greatest consolation that I was capable of receiving. They elevated me from all littleness of feeling, and although they did not remove my grief, they subdued and tranquillized it.

entries.what: The narrator retired to rest at night, and his slumbers were ministered to by the grand shapes he had contemplated during the day.
entries.quote: I retired to rest at night; my slumbers, as it were, waited on and ministered to by the assemblance of grand shapes which I had contemplated during the day.

entries.what: The next morning, the narrator awoke to find the soul-inspiriting scenes had fled with sleep, and dark melancholy clouded every thought.
entries.quote: Where had they fled when the next morning I awoke? All of soul-inspiriting fled with sleep, and dark melancholy clouded every thought.

entries.what: The narrator resolved to ascend to the summit of Montanvert to recapture the joy he had previously felt from the glacier view.
entries.quote: I resolved to ascend to the summit of Montanvert.

entries.what: The ascent to Montanvert is precipitous with a path cut into continual and short windings, and is intersected by snow ravines where stones roll down.
entries.quote: The ascent is precipitous, but the path is cut into continual and short windings, which enable you to surmount the perpendicularity of the mountain. It is a scene terrifically desolate. In a thousand spots the traces of the winter avalanche may be perceived...

entries.what: The narrator reached the top of the ascent near noon and sat upon a rock overlooking the sea of ice.
entries.quote: It was nearly noon when I arrived at the top of the ascent. For some time I sat upon the rock that overlooks the sea of ice.

entries.what: The narrator descended onto the glacier and observed its uneven surface, rifts, and the opposite mountain's perpendicular rock face.
entries.quote: The surface is very uneven, rising like the waves of a troubled sea, descending low, and interspersed by rifts that sink deep.

entries.what: The narrator gazed at Mont Blanc in awful majesty and felt his heart swell with something like joy, exclaiming to wandering spirits.
entries.quote: My heart, which was before sorrowful, now swelled with something like joy; I exclaimed, 'Wandering spirits, if indeed ye wander, and do not rest in your narrow beds, allow me this faint happiness, or take me, as your companion, away from the joys of life.'

entries.what: The narrator suddenly beheld the figure of a man advancing towards him with superhuman speed across the ice.
entries.quote: As I said this I suddenly beheld the figure of a man, at some distance, advancing towards me with superhuman speed.

entries.what: The narrator recognized the figure as the wretch he had created, feeling terror and rage upon the realization.
entries.quote: I perceived, as the shape came nearer (sight tremendous and abhorred!) that it was the wretch whom I had created.

entries.what: The narrator resolved to wait the creature's approach and then close with him in mortal combat.
entries.quote: I trembled with rage and horror, resolving to wait his approach and then close with him in mortal combat.

entries.what: The creature spoke, expressing that all men hate the wretched and asking why he must be hated more than all living things.
entries.quote: I expected this reception,

entries.what: The creature pleads with the narrator to listen to his tale before passing judgment, claiming he was benevolent but made a fiend by misery.
entries.quote: Have I not suffered enough, that you seek to increase my misery? Life, although it may only be an accumulation of anguish, is dear to me, and I will defend it.

entries.what: The creature requests the narrator to perform his duty toward him, promising to leave the narrator and mankind in peace if the narrator complies with his conditions.
entries.quote: If you will comply with my conditions, I will leave them and you at peace; but if you refuse, I will glut the maw of death, until it be satiated with the blood of your remaining friends.

entries.what: The narrator refuses to listen, declaring they are enemies and challenging the creature to a fight.
entries.quote: Abhorred monster! Fiend that thou art! The tortures of hell are too mild a vengeance for thy crimes. Wretched devil! You reproach me with your creation, come on, then, that I may extinguish the spark which I so negligently bestowed.

entries.what: The creature entreats the narrator to hear him out, arguing that the guilty are allowed to speak in their own defence before condemnation.
entries.quote: The guilty are allowed, by human laws, bloody as they are, to speak in their own defence before they are condemned.

entries.what: The creature begs the narrator to have compassion and not disdain him, offering to lead a harmless life if the narrator listens to his tale.
entries.quote: Listen to my tale; it is long and strange, and the temperature of this place is not fitting to your fine sensations; come to the hut upon the mountain.

entries.what: The narrator, partly by curiosity and compassion, agrees to hear the creature's tale.
entries.quote: I was partly urged by curiosity, and compassion confirmed my resolution.

entries.what: The narrator and the creature cross the ice and ascend the opposite rock, entering a hut as rain begins to descend.
entries.when: We crossed the ice, therefore, and ascended the opposite rock
entries.quote: We crossed the ice, therefore, and ascended the opposite rock. The air was cold, and the rain again began to descend; we entered the hut...

entries.what: The creature awakens in the forest near Ingolstadt, disoriented and overwhelmed by sensory input, and learns to distinguish sensations over time.
entries.when: Upon first awakening; time unspecified but shortly after creation.
entries.why: The creature's senses were initially confused; it took time to learn to distinguish between operations of the various senses.
entries.quote: It is with considerable difficulty that I remember the original era of my being; all the events of that period appear confused and indistinct.

entries.what: The creature finds shade and rests by a brook in the forest near Ingolstadt, eats berries, and slakes thirst before falling asleep.
entries.when: After wandering and discovering the forest near Ingolstadt; time unspecified.
entries.why: The creature was weary from walking and sought shade; hunger and thirst roused it from a nearly dormant state.
entries.quote: I walked and, I believe, descended, but I presently found a great alteration in my sensations. Before, dark and opaque bodies had surrounded me... but I now found that I could wander on at liberty... I sought a place where I could receive shade. This was the forest near Ingolstadt; and here I lay by the side of a brook resting from my fatigue...

entries.what: The creature observes the moon for the first time and feels pleasure from its light, which enlightens its path.
entries.when: When the creature awoke in the forest at night after sleeping by the brook.
entries.why: A gentle light stole over the heavens, giving the creature a sensation of pleasure; it saw a radiant form rise from among the trees.
entries.quote: Soon a gentle light stole over the heavens and gave me a sensation of pleasure. I started up and beheld a radiant form rise from among the trees.

entries.what: The creature discovers fire left by beggars, experiences warmth, and is burned when thrusting hand into live embers.
entries.when: One day when the creature was oppressed by cold; time unspecified.
entries.why: The creature found delight in the warmth of the fire but was overcome with pain when its hand entered the live embers, learning that the same cause produces opposite effects.
entries.quote: One day, when I was oppressed by cold, I found a fire which had been left by some wandering beggars, and was overcome with delight at the warmth I experienced from it. In my joy I thrust my hand into the live embers, but quickly drew it out again with a cry of pain.

entries.what: The creature learns to manage fire by drying wet wood and uses it to roast food, finding roasted offals more savory than berries.
entries.when: After discovering fire; later that night and following mornings.
entries.why: The creature observed that wet wood dried and became inflamed by the heat; it collected wood to dry it and have a plentiful supply of fire. It found roasted offals tasted much more savory than berries.
entries.quote: The wet wood which I had placed near the heat dried and itself became inflamed. I reflected on this, and by touching the various branches, I discovered the cause and busied myself in collecting a great quantity of wood, that I might dry it and have a plentiful supply of fire.

entries.what: The creature leaves the forest and discovers a shepherd's hut, enters it, eats the remnants of the shepherd's breakfast, and falls asleep on straw.
entries.when: After traveling through the snow; morning unspecified but after a great fall of snow the night before.
entries.why: The creature longed to obtain food and shelter; it found a hut on rising ground built for a shepherd's convenience and greedily devoured the remnants of his breakfast.
entries.quote: At length I perceived a small hut, on a rising ground, which had doubtless been built for the convenience of some shepherd. Finding the door open, I entered. An old man sat in it, near a fire, over which he was preparing his breakfast.

entries.what: The creature observes the cottagers through a chink in the wall, noting their interactions, the old man playing an instrument, and the young girl's sad demeanor.
entries.when: During the creature's residence in the hovel; time unspecified but over several days.
entries.why: The creature arranged its dwelling and observed the cottage; it saw a young creature with a pail, a young man with melancholy countenance, and the old man playing an instrument that produced sweet sounds.
entries.quote: In one of these was a small and almost imperceptible chink through which the eye could just penetrate. Through this crevice a small room was visible, whitewashed and clean but very bare of furniture. In one corner, near a small fire, sat an old man, leaning his head on his hands in a disconsolate attitude.

entries.what: The creature witnesses the young man reading aloud to the young woman, producing monotonous sounds, while the old man plays mournful music that moves her to tears.
entries.when: In the evening while the cottagers are occupied before resting.
entries.why: The young man uttered monotonous sounds, which the creature later learned was reading aloud; the old man played a sweet mournful air that drew tears from the young woman's eyes.
entries.quote: The old man again took up the instrument which produced the divine sounds that had enchanted me in the morning. So soon as he had finished, the youth began, not to play, but to utter sounds that were monotonous... I since found that he read aloud, but at that time I knew nothing of the science of words or letters.

entries.what: The creature flees the village after being attacked by inhabitants, bruised by stones, and seeks refuge in a bare hovel.
entries.when: At sunset after arriving at a village; evening of the same day.
entries.why: One of the best cottages the creature entered caused children to shriek and a woman to faint; the village was roused, some fled, some attacked the creature with stones and missile weapons.
entries.quote: One of the best of these I entered, but I had hardly placed my foot within the door before the children shrieked, and one of the women fainted. The whole village was roused; some fled, some attacked me, until, grievously bruised by stones and many other kinds of missile weapons, I escaped to the open country.

entries.what: The creature prepares a sheltered hovel using stones and wood to cover creches, carpeting it with clean straw and keeping dry from rain and snow.
entries.when: After fleeing the village; morning after the creature's arrival at the hovel.
entries.why: The creature covered every crevice with stones and wood to avoid being perceived; it carpeted the dwelling with clean straw for comfort.
entries.quote: Having thus arranged my dwelling and carpeted it with clean straw, I retired, for I saw the figure of a man at a distance, and I remembered too well my treatment the night before to trust myself in his power.

entries.what: The creature observes a young girl fetching milk and a young man helping her, noting their gentle demeanor and the young man's melancholy countenance.
entries.when: Morning while the creature resides in the hovel; time unspecified but during the day.
entries.why: The creature saw a young creature with a pail passing by; the girl was young and of gentle demeanor, the young man had a countenance expressing deeper despondence and took the pail from her head.
entries.quote: I beheld a young creature, with a pail on her head, passing before my hovel. The girl was young and of gentle demeanour, unlike what I have since found cottagers and farmhouse servants to be.

entries.what: The creature lies on straw and cannot sleep, thinking of the day's events and the gentle manners of the cottagers, but dares not join them due to past mistreatment by villagers.
entries.quote: I lay on my straw, but I could not sleep. I thought of the occurrences of the day. What chiefly struck me was the gentle manners of these people, and I longed to join them, but dared not.

entries.what: The cottagers arise before the sun; the young woman arranges the cottage and prepares food, and the youth departs after the first meal.
