entries.quote: The cottagers arose the next morning before the sun. The young woman arranged the cottage and prepared the food, and the youth departed after the first meal.

entries.what: The young man and his companion often go apart and appear to weep, though the creature cannot initially understand the cause of their unhappiness.
entries.quote: The young man and his companion often went apart and appeared to weep. I saw no cause for their unhappiness, but I was deeply affected by it.

entries.what: The creature discovers the cottagers are poor; their nourishment consists of garden vegetables and milk from one cow, which gives little during winter, causing them to suffer distressing hunger.
entries.quote: A considerable period elapsed before I discovered one of the causes of the uneasiness of this amiable family: it was poverty, and they suffered that evil in a very distressing degree. Their nourishment consisted entirely of the vegetables of their garden and the milk of one cow, which gave very little during the winter.

entries.what: The creature stops stealing the cottagers' food after realizing it causes them pain, and instead satisfies himself with berries, nuts, and roots from the neighboring wood.
entries.quote: I had been accustomed, during the night, to steal a part of their store for my own consumption, but when I found that in doing this I inflicted pain on the cottagers, I abstained and satisfied myself with berries, nuts, and roots which I gathered from a neighbouring wood.

entries.what: The creature secretly brings wood to the cottage at night using Felix's tools, enabling the youth to spend the day repairing the cottage and cultivating the garden instead of collecting wood.
entries.quote: I often took his tools, the use of which I quickly discovered, and brought home firing sufficient for the consumption of several days.

entries.what: The creature discovers the cottagers communicate through articulate sounds (language), which he perceives as a godlike science, and he ardently desires to learn it.
entries.quote: I found that these people possessed a method of communicating their experience and feelings to one another by articulate sounds. I perceived that the words they spoke sometimes produced pleasure or pain, smiles or sadness, in the minds and countenances of the hearers.

entries.what: The creature learns the names of familiar objects and the cottagers: 'fire,' 'milk,' 'bread,' 'wood,' 'father,' 'Agatha,' and 'Felix.'
entries.quote: By great application, however, and after having remained during the space of several revolutions of the moon in my hovel, I discovered the names that were given to some of the most familiar objects of discourse; I learned and applied the words, 'fire,' 'milk,' 'bread,' and 'wood.'

entries.what: The creature spends the winter observing the cottagers, feeling depressed when they are unhappy and sympathizing in their joys, and regarding them as superior beings who will arbitrate his future destiny.
entries.quote: I spent the winter in this manner. The gentle manners and beauty of the cottagers greatly endeared them to me; when they were unhappy, I felt depressed; when they rejoiced, I sympathized in their joys.

entries.what: The creature resolves to learn the cottagers' language before revealing himself, believing it might enable them to overlook his deformity.
entries.quote: I ought not to make the attempt until I had first become master of their language, which knowledge might enable me to make them overlook the deformity of my figure.

entries.what: The creature is horrified upon seeing his own reflection in a transparent pool, realizing he is the monster he is, and feels despondence and mortification.
entries.quote: I had admired the perfect forms of my cottagers--their grace, beauty, and delicate complexions; but how was I terrified when I viewed myself in a transparent pool! When I became fully convinced that I was in reality the monster that I am, I was filled with the bitterest sensations of despondence and mortification.

entries.what: With the arrival of spring, the cottagers' food becomes more sufficient, and Felix is more employed; the signs of impending famine disappear.
entries.quote: As the sun became warmer and the light of day longer, the snow vanished, and I beheld the bare trees and the black earth. From this time Felix was more employed, and the heart-moving indications of impending famine disappeared.

entries.what: The old man takes a daily walk with his son Felix at noon when it does not rain, which frequently happens but is quickly dried by a high wind.
entries.quote: The old man, leaning on his son, walked each day at noon, when it did not rain, as I found it was called when the heavens poured forth its waters.

entries.what: The creature performs acts of service for the cottagers at night, such as clearing snow from paths and bringing wood, which astonishes them and leads them to utter the words 'good spirit' and 'wonderful' without understanding their meaning.
entries.quote: I cleared their path from the snow and performed those offices that I had seen done by Felix. I afterwards found that these labours, performed by an invisible hand, greatly astonished them; and once or twice I heard them, on these occasions, utter the words 'good spirit,' 'wonderful'.

entries.what: The creature becomes inquisitive about why Felix appears miserable and Agatha sad, thinking it might be in his power to restore happiness to them, and forms images of presenting himself to them.
entries.quote: I was inquisitive to know why Felix appeared so miserable and Agatha so sad. I thought (foolish wretch!) that it might be in my power to restore happiness to these deserving people.

entries.what: The creature applies himself fresh ardor to learning the cottagers' language, noting his organs are harsh but supple, and his voice unlike their soft music, yet he can pronounce words he understands with tolerable ease.
entries.quote: My organs were indeed harsh, but supple; and although my voice was very unlike the soft music of their tones, yet I pronounced such words as I understood with tolerable ease.

entries.what: The creature observes the transformative effect of spring on nature and feels his spirits elevated, regarding the past as blotted from memory and the future gilded by hope and anticipations of joy.
entries.quote: The pleasant showers and genial warmth of spring greatly altered the aspect of the earth. My spirits were elevated by the enchanting appearance of nature; the past was blotted from my memory, the present was tranquil, and the future gilded by bright rays of hope and anticipations of joy.

entries.what: The cottagers rest from labor, and the old man plays guitar while the children listen.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: It was on one of these days, when my cottagers periodically rested from labour--the old man played on his guitar, and the children listened to him--

entries.what: Felix appears melancholy, sighs frequently, and his father pauses music, inquiring into his sorrow.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: I observed the countenance of Felix was melancholy beyond expression; he sighed frequently, and once his father paused in his music, and I conjectured by his manner that he inquired the cause of his son's sorrow.

entries.what: A lady on horseback, accompanied by a countryman, arrives at the cottage; she wears a dark suit and thick black veil.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: It was a lady on horseback, accompanied by a country-man as a guide. The lady was dressed in a dark suit and covered with a thick black veil.

entries.what: The stranger's name is Safie; she is Felix's 'sweet Arabian' and possesses angelic beauty with raven black hair and gentle dark eyes.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: On hearing this word, Felix came up hastily to the lady, who, when she saw him, threw up her veil, and I beheld a countenance of angelic beauty and expression. Her hair of a shining raven black, and curiously braided; her eyes were dark, but gentle, although animated;

entries.what: Safie does not understand the cottagers' language, and they do not understand hers, but her presence diffuses gladness through the cottage.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: Although the stranger uttered articulate sounds and appeared to have a language of her own, she was neither understood by nor herself understood the cottagers. They made many signs which I did not comprehend, but I saw that her presence diffused gladness through the cottage, dispelling their sorrow as the sun dissipates the morning mists.

entries.what: Safie attempts to learn the cottagers' language, repeating sounds after them, and the narrator resolves to learn the same way.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: I soon perceived that although the stranger uttered articulate sounds and appeared to have a language of her own, she was neither understood by nor herself understood the cottagers... the idea instantly occurred to me that I should make use of the same instructions to the same end.

entries.what: Safie learns about twenty words at the first lesson, most of which the narrator had previously understood.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: The stranger learned about twenty words at the first lesson; most of them, indeed, were those which I had before understood, but I profited by the others.

entries.what: Safie plays the guitar and sings with a rich cadence, drawing tears of sorrow and delight; the old man is enraptured.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: after the usual occupations of Agatha were finished, the Arabian sat at the feet of the old man, and taking his guitar, played some airs so entrancingly beautiful that they at once drew tears of sorrow and delight from my eyes. She sang, and her voice flowed in a rich cadence, swelling or dying away like a nightingale of the woods.

entries.what: The narrator studies Volney's Ruins of Empires, instructed by Felix, and gains a view of world history, empires, manners, governments, and religions.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: The book from which Felix instructed Safie was Volney's Ruins of Empires. I should not have understood the purport of this book had not Felix, in reading it, given very minute explanations.

entries.what: The narrator learns about human society: division of property, immense wealth and squalid poverty, rank, descent, and noble blood.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: I heard of the division of property, of immense wealth and squalid poverty, of rank, descent, and noble blood.

entries.what: The narrator reflects on his own wretched condition, feeling deformed and alone, with no money, friends, or property, and wonders if he is a monster.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: I was, besides, endued with a figure hideously deformed and loathsome; I was not even of the same nature as man. I was more agile than they and could subsist upon coarser diet; I bore the extremes of heat and cold with less injury to my frame; my stature far exceeded theirs. When I looked around I saw and heard of none like me. Was I, then, a monster, a blot upon the earth, from which all men fled and whom all men disowned?

entries.what: The narrator learns about the differences of sexes, birth and growth of children, and family relationships such as father, mother, brother, and sister.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: I heard of the difference of sexes, and the birth and growth of children, how the father doted on the smiles of the infant, and the lively sallies of the older child, how all the life and cares of the mother were wrapped up in the precious charge, how the mind of youth expanded and gained knowledge, of brother, sister, and all the various relationships which bind one human being to another in mutual bonds.

entries.what: The narrator feels shut out from the cottagers, experiencing the gentle words of Agatha and smiles of Safie as not meant for him, leading to misery.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: The gentle words of Agatha and the animated smiles of the charming Arabian were not for me. The mild exhortations of the old man and the lively conversation of the loved Felix were not for me. Miserable, unhappy wretch!

entries.what: The narrator improves rapidly in language comprehension, outpacing Safie, who understands very little and speaks in broken accents.
entries.when: during Spring, when the weather became fine and skies cloudless
entries.quote: I may boast that I improved more rapidly than the Arabian, who understood very little and conversed in broken accents, whilst I comprehended and could imitate almost every word that was spoken.

entries.what: The old man's name was De Lacey, descended from a good family in France, who lived in affluence and was respected and beloved before their ruin.
entries.quote: The name of the old man was De Lacey. He was descended from a good family in France, where he had lived for many years in affluence, respected by his superiors and beloved by his equals.

entries.what: The father of Safie was a Turkish merchant who was imprisoned and condemned to death due to his religion and wealth rather than the crime alleged against him.
entries.quote: He was a Turkish merchant and had inhabited Paris for many years, when, for some reason which I could not learn, he became obnoxious to the government. He was seized and cast into prison the very day that Safie arrived from Constantinople to join him. He was tried and condemned to death.

entries.what: Felix accidentally witnessed the trial of the Turkish merchant and vowed to deliver him, later finding a grated window to communicate with the prisoner at night.
entries.quote: Felix had accidentally been present at the trial; his horror and indignation were uncontrollable when he heard the decision of the court. He made, at that moment, a solemn vow to deliver him and then looked around for the means.

entries.what: Felix smuggled the Turkish merchant out of prison through a grated window and helped him escape to Lyons and then across Mont Cenis to Leghorn.
entries.quote: After many fruitless attempts to gain admittance to the prison, he found a strongly grated window in an unguarded part of the building, which lighted the dungeon of the unfortunate Muhammadan, who, loaded with chains, waited in despair the execution of the barbarous sentence.

entries.what: Safie fell in love with Felix after seeing him visit her father in prison and observing his noble intentions, desiring to marry him and remain in a country where women have rights.
entries.quote: The Turk, amazed and delighted, endeavoured to kindle the zeal of his deliverer by promises of reward and wealth. Felix rejected his offers with contempt, yet when he saw the lovely Safie, who was allowed to visit her father and who by her gestures expressed her lively gratitude, the youth could not help owning to his own mind that the captive possessed a treasure which would fully reward his toil and hazard.

entries.what: Felix and Safie carried on a romantic correspondence through letters facilitated by an old servant who understood French, deepening their affection before they met.
entries.quote: During the ensuing days, while the preparations were going forward for the escape of the merchant, the zeal of Felix was warmed by several letters that he received from this lovely girl, who found means to express her thoughts in the language of her lover by the aid of an old man, a servant of her father who understood French.

entries.what: The Turkish merchant escaped from prison the night before his execution, and Felix helped his family flee Paris using forged passports.
entries.quote: The day for the execution of the Turk was fixed, but on the night previous to it he quitted his prison and before morning was distant many leagues from Paris. Felix had procured passports in the name of his father, sister, and himself.

entries.what: De Lacey and Agatha were imprisoned and eventually exiled permanently after Felix surrendered himself to save them, losing their fortune in the process.
entries.quote: His blind and aged father and his gentle sister lay in a noisome dungeon while he enjoyed the free air and the society of her whom he loved. This idea was torture to him. He quickly arranged with the Turk that if the latter should find a favourable opportunity for escape before Felix could return to Italy, Safie should remain as a boarder at a convent at Leghorn; and then, quitting the lovely Arabian, he hastened to Paris and delivered himself up to the vengeance of the law, hoping to free De Lacey and Agatha by this proceeding.

entries.what: The Turkish merchant betrayed Felix by leaving Italy with Safie and sending only a small pittance of money, showing ingratitude for Felix's sacrifice.
entries.quote: The treacherous Turk, for whom he and his family endured such unheard-of oppression, on discovering that his deliverer was thus reduced to poverty and ruin, became a traitor to good feeling and honour and had quitted Italy with his daughter, insultingly sending Felix a pittance of money to aid him, as he said, in some plan of future maintenance.

entries.what: Safie fled to Germany to be with Felix after learning of his exile and her father's intention to take her back to Turkey, overcoming the loss of her attendant to reach the cottage.
entries.quote: She arrived in safety at a town about twenty leagues from the cottage of De Lacey, when her attendant fell dangerously ill. Safie nursed her with the most devoted affection, but the poor girl died, and the Arabian was left alone, unacquainted with the language of the country and utterly ignorant of the customs of the world.

entries.what: The creature finds a leathern portmanteau containing clothes and books (Paradise Lost, Plutarch's Lives, and Sorrows of Werter) in the woods.
entries.when: Beginning of the month of August
entries.why: The creature collected food and firing for his protectors when he found the portmanteau.
entries.quote: One night during my accustomed visit to the neighbouring wood where I collected my own food and brought home firing for my protectors, I found on the ground a leathern portmanteau containing several articles of dress and some books.

entries.what: The creature reads Paradise Lost and views it as true history, identifying with Adam's solitary state.
entries.when: After finding the books in August
entries.why: The creature relates to Adam's creation and isolation, feeling wretched and alone like Adam but without his blessed state.
entries.quote: Like Adam, I was apparently united by no link to any other being in existence; but his state was far different from mine in every other respect.

entries.what: The creature reads Sorrows of Werter and identifies with Werter's gloom and envy toward his protectors' bliss.
entries.when: After finding the books in August
entries.why: The creature finds Werter's character divine and sinks deep, feeling envy when viewing his protectors' happiness.
entries.quote: But I thought Werter himself a more divine being than I had ever beheld or imagined; his character contained no pretension, but it sank deep.

entries.what: The creature reads Plutarch's Lives and admires virtuous lawgivers like Numa, Solon, and Lycurgus over Romulus and Theseus.
entries.when: After finding the books in August
entries.why: Plutarch taught the creature high thoughts and elevated him above his wretched reflections, inspiring admiration for peaceable lawgivers.
entries.quote: I felt the greatest ardour for virtue rise within me, and abhorrence for vice... Induced by these feelings, I was of course led to admire peaceable lawgivers, Numa, Solon, and Lycurgus.

entries.what: The creature discovers Victor's journal in the pocket of the dress taken from the laboratory.
entries.when: Soon after arriving in the hovel
entries.why: The creature found papers in the pocket of the dress he had taken, which turned out to be Victor's journal of the four months preceding his creation.
entries.quote: Soon after my arrival in the hovel I discovered some papers in the pocket of the dress which I had taken from your laboratory.

entries.what: The creature feels indignation and despair upon reading Victor's journal detailing his creation.
entries.why: The journal describes the 'disgusting circumstances' of his creation and renders his 'form indelible' in his mind, causing agony and self-loathing.
entries.quote: Hateful day when I received life! I exclaimed in agony. Accursed creator! Why did you form a monster so hideous that even YOU turned from me in disgust?

entries.what: The creature resolves to seek the cottagers' protection and kindness, hoping they will overlook his deformity if they know his good dispositions.
entries.when: During his despondent reflections after reading the books and journal
entries.why: The creature believes the cottagers are prejudiced against his person but will pity his 'amiable and benevolent dispositions' and 'harmless' life.
entries.quote: I tenderly love these friends; I have, unknown to them, been for many months in the habits of daily kindness towards them; but they believe that I wish to injure them.

entries.what: The creature decides to approach the old De Lacey alone when his children are away, hoping the blind man cannot judge his countenance.
entries.when: Autumn, after a full revolution of seasons since he awoke
entries.why: The creature knows his 'unnatural hideousness' is the chief object of horror, but thinks his voice is not terrible and that gaining the old man's goodwill might secure tolerance from the younger protectors.
entries.quote: I had sagacity enough to discover that the unnatural hideousness of my person was the chief object of horror with those who had formerly beheld me.

entries.what: The creature enters the cottage and speaks with the old De Lacey, who offers friendship based on sincerity of words despite blindness to his appearance.
entries.when: One day when Safie, Agatha, and Felix are away on a long walk
entries.why: The old man is blind and cannot judge the creature's countenance, and something in the creature's words persuades him of his sincerity.
entries.quote: By your language, stranger, I suppose you are my countryman; are you French?

entries.what: The creature reveals his true identity and plea for protection to De Lacey just as Felix, Safie, and Agatha return.
entries.why: The creature seizes the moment to cry 'Now is the time! Save and protect me!' before the children enter and react with horror.
entries.quote: Now is the time! Save and protect me! You and your family are the friends whom I seek. Do not you desert me in the hour of trial!

entries.what: Felix attacks the creature with a stick, causing him to flee the cottage in pain and anguish.
entries.when: When Felix, Safie, and Agatha enter the cottage
entries.why: Felix is overcome by fury at seeing the creature with his father and uses supernatural force to dash him to the ground and strike him violently.
entries.quote: Felix darted forward, and with supernatural force tore me from his father, to whose knees I clung, in a transport of fury, he dashed me to the ground and struck me violently with a stick.

entries.what: The creature declares everlasting war against the species and especially against his creator after being spurned by the De Lacey family.
entries.when: After being chased away from the cottage and reflecting on his treatment, during the night he spends in the woods.
entries.why: The creature feels unsympathized with and declares war after his attempt to befriend the De Laceys is rejected.
entries.quote: I declared everlasting war against the species, and more than all, against him who had formed me and sent me forth to this insupportable misery.

entries.what: The creature resolves to return to the cottage to win over the old De Lacey first, hoping the family will then accept him.
entries.when: During the afternoon after his first rejection, before he falls into a profound sleep.
entries.why: He realizes he acted imprudently by exposing himself to the children and decides to familiarize the old man first.
entries.quote: I ought to have familiarized the old De Lacey to me, and by degrees to have discovered myself to the rest of his family, when they should have been prepared for my approach.

entries.what: The creature burns down the De Lacey cottage in a fit of rage after being rejected and wounded by a rustic.
entries.when: At night, after the moon has sunk, while the creature is in a state of forced impatience and fury.
entries.why: The creature feels betrayed by humanity; after saving a girl and being shot, he resolves to destroy the cottage and all cultivation in the garden.
entries.quote: I lighted the dry branch of a tree and danced with fury around the devoted cottage... I fired the straw, and the heath, and bushes, which I had collected.

entries.what: The creature resolves to travel to Geneva to seek his creator, Victor Frankenstein, for pity and redress.
entries.when: After leaving the De Lacey family, during his long travel in autumn and winter.
entries.why: He learned from Victor's papers that Victor is his creator and feels he can only hope for succor from him despite his hatred.
entries.quote: I learned from your papers that you were my father, my creator; and to whom could I apply with more fitness than to him who had given me life?

entries.what: The creature saves a young girl from drowning in a river but is shot by a rustic who sees him, leading to his wound and rage.
entries.when: One morning in spring, when he ventures out after sunrise and comes to a deep rapid river.
entries.why: The creature rushes to save the girl from the current, but a rustic aims a gun at him and fires when he approaches.
entries.quote: I rushed from my hiding-place and with extreme labour, from the force of the current, saved her and dragged her to shore.

entries.what: The creature murders a young boy, William Frankenstein, after the boy screams upon seeing his form and threatens to call his father, M. Frankenstein.
entries.when: After wandering towards the mountains and encountering the boy on a path near Geneva, during his travel towards Geneva.
entries.why: The creature decides the boy is the son of his enemy Victor Frankenstein and killing him will cause his creator despair.
entries.quote: Frankenstein! you belong then to my enemy--to him towards whom I have sworn eternal revenge; you shall be my first victim.

entries.what: The creature places a portrait of a lovely woman into the dress of a sleeping woman in a barn, then flees when she stirs.
entries.when: After murdering William Frankenstein, he hides in a barn and encounters a young woman sleeping there.
entries.why: In his rage and misery, he decides the woman will suffer for the joys he is deprived of; he steals the portrait to punish her.
entries.quote: I bent over her and placed the portrait securely in one of the folds of her dress. She moved again, and I fled.

entries.what: The creature resolves to demand that Victor create a female companion for him, threatening to destroy Victor's life if he refuses.
entries.when: After weeks of wandering in the woods and reaching the environs of Geneva, before he sees the child.
entries.why: He is alone and miserable; man will not associate with him, but a being of the same species would not deny herself to him.
entries.quote: My companion must be of the same species and have the same defects. This being you must create.

entries.what: The creature demands that Victor create a female companion for him so he can live in sympathy and avoid further misery.
entries.why: The creature argues he is malicious because he is miserable and shunned by all mankind; he promises to leave Europe forever if granted a companion.
entries.quote: "You must create a female for me with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being."

entries.what: Victor initially refuses the creature's demand, declaring he will never consent to create another like him.
entries.why: Victor fears the joint wickedness of two creatures could desolate the world and refuses to be base in his own eyes.
entries.quote: "I do refuse it," I replied; "and no torture shall ever extort a consent from me."

entries.what: The creature argues he is malicious because he is miserable and rejected by all mankind, including his creator.
entries.why: He claims Victor would destroy him if given the chance and questions why he should pity man when man pities him not.
entries.quote: "I am malicious because I am miserable. Am I not shunned and hated by all mankind?"

entries.what: The creature promises to quit the neighbourhood of man and dwell in the wilds of South America if Victor grants his request.
entries.why: He swears that with a companion he will meet with sympathy and his life will flow quietly away without cursing his maker.
entries.quote: "I swear... that with the companion you bestow I will quit the neighbourhood of man and dwell, as it may chance, in the most savage of places."

entries.what: Victor eventually consents to create the female creature, on condition that the creature swears to quit Europe forever after receiving her.
entries.why: Victor reflects on the justice due to the creature and his fellow creatures, and fears the creature's power to hide in ice caves and inaccessible precipices.
entries.quote: "I consent to your demand, on your solemn oath to quit Europe forever, and every other place in the neighbourhood of man, as soon as I shall deliver into your hands a female who will accompany you in your exile."

entries.what: The creature swears on the sun, blue sky, and fire of love that he will never be seen again if his prayer is granted.
entries.why: He promises to depart and be unseen while the conditions exist, watching Victor's progress with unutterable anxiety.
entries.quote: "I swear... by the sun, and by the blue sky of heaven, and by the fire of love that burns my heart, that if you grant my prayer, while they exist you shall never behold me again."

entries.what: The creature flees the mountain after making his vow, descending with greater speed than an eagle and losing himself among the sea of ice.
entries.why: He is fearful of any change in Victor's sentiments after making his promise.
entries.quote: Saying this, he suddenly quitted me, fearful, perhaps, of any change in my sentiments. I saw him descend the mountain with greater speed than the flight of an eagle...

entries.what: Victor spends the night on the mountain after the creature's departure, weeping and contemplating the darkness and solitude around him.
entries.why: He is overwhelmed by emotions from the day's events and feels crushed by the eternal twinkling of the stars and winds.
entries.quote: I wept bitterly, and clasping my hands in agony, I exclaimed, "Oh! Stars and clouds and winds, ye are all about to mock me; if ye really pity me, crush sensation and memory; let me become as nought; but if not, depart, depart, and leave me in darkness."

entries.what: Victor returns to Geneva the next morning without resting, feeling weighed down by his sensations and unable to express them.
entries.why: He arrives at the village of Chamounix at dawn and immediately returns to Geneva, feeling a mountain's weight of emotion.
entries.quote: Morning dawned before I arrived at the village of Chamounix; I took no rest, but returned immediately to Geneva.

entries.what: Victor resolves to dedicate himself to the abhorred task of creating the female creature to save his family from the creature's vengeance.
entries.why: Even though he feels under a ban and cannot claim their sympathies, he loves the family to adoration and resolves to save them.
entries.quote: Yet even thus I loved them to adoration; and to save them, I resolved to dedicate myself to my most abhorred task.

entries.what: Victor fears the vengeance of the disappointed fiend and is unable to overcome his repugnance to resuming his work on creating a female companion.
entries.quote: I could not collect the courage to recommence my work. I feared the vengeance of the disappointed fiend, yet I was unable to overcome my repugnance to the task which was enjoined me.

entries.what: Victor cannot compose a female without devoting several months to profound study and laborious disquisition.
entries.quote: I found that I could not compose a female without again devoting several months to profound study and laborious disquisition.

entries.what: Victor considers visiting England to obtain knowledge from an English philosopher that is material to his success.
entries.quote: I had heard of some discoveries having been made by an English philosopher, the knowledge of which was material to my success, and I sometimes thought of obtaining my father's consent to visit England for this purpose.

entries.what: Victor's father observes a change in Victor's health and spirits, and suspects Victor may regard Elizabeth as a sister or have met another woman he loves.
entries.quote: I confess, my son, that I have always looked forward to your marriage with our dear Elizabeth as the tie of our domestic comfort and the stay of my declining years. You were attached to each other from your earliest infancy...

entries.what: Victor reassures his father that he loves Elizabeth tenderly and that his future hopes are bound up in their union.
entries.quote: My dear father, reassure yourself. I love my cousin tenderly and sincerely. I never saw any woman who excited, as Elizabeth does, my warmest admiration and affection.

entries.what: Victor feels that an immediate marriage with Elizabeth would be horror and dismay because he is bound by a solemn promise to create the monster a mate first.
entries.quote: I was bound by a solemn promise which I had not yet fulfilled and dared not break, or if I did, what manifold miseries might not impend over me and my devoted family! Could I enter into a festival with this deadly weight yet hanging round my neck and bowing me to the ground?

entries.what: Victor wishes to visit England to obtain the necessary knowledge for his task, concealing the true reasons from his father.
entries.quote: I expressed a wish to visit England, but concealing the true reasons of this request, I clothed my desires under a guise which excited no suspicion.

entries.what: Victor's father had arranged for Clerval to join Victor at Strasbourg without previously communicating with Victor.
entries.quote: Without previously communicating with me, he had, in concert with Elizabeth, arranged that Clerval should join me at Strasbourg.

entries.what: Victor departs for England in the latter end of September.
entries.quote: It was in the latter end of September that I again quitted my native country.

entries.what: Elizabeth is filled with disquiet at the idea of Victor suffering away from her and longs to bid him hasten his return.
entries.quote: She longed to bid me hasten my return; a thousand conflicting emotions rendered her mute as she bade me a tearful, silent farewell.

entries.what: Victor and Clerval travel down the Rhine from Strasbourg to Rotterdam, passing through Mannheim and Mainz, and enjoy the scenic landscape including ruined castles and vineyards.
entries.quote: During this voyage we passed many willowy islands and saw several beautiful towns. We stayed a day at Mannheim, and on the fifth from our departure from Strasbourg, arrived at Mainz.

entries.what: Victor and Clerval travel by sea from Rotterdam to England, arriving on a clear morning in the latter days of December and seeing the white cliffs of Britain.
entries.quote: It was on a clear morning, in the latter days of December, that I first saw the white cliffs of Britain.

entries.what: Victor sees London's numerous steeples, St. Paul's towering above all, and the Tower famed in English history as he arrives in the city.
entries.quote: At length we saw the numerous steeples of London, St. Paul's towering above all, and the Tower famed in English history.

entries.what: Victor and Clerval travel to London to seek information for Victor's project, staying several months.
entries.when: After passing some months in London, they receive a letter from Scotland in February.
entries.why: Victor needs information to complete his promise; Clerval desires to meet men of genius and talent.
entries.quote: London was our present point of rest; we determined to remain several months in this wonderful and celebrated city.

entries.what: Victor is consumed by anguish and isolates himself from Clerval, fearing the monster's vengeance on his relatives.
entries.when: After arriving in England at the beginning of October, it is now February; they plan a northern journey ending about July.
entries.why: A blight has come over Victor's existence; he feels an insurmountable barrier from fellow men sealed with the blood of William and Justine.
entries.quote: But a blight had come over my existence, and I only visited these people for the sake of the information they might give me.

entries.what: Clerval plans to visit India to assist European colonization and trade using his knowledge of languages and society.
entries.when: During their time in London, before their northern journey.
entries.why: Clerval believes he can materially assist the progress of European colonization and trade through his views of Indian society.
entries.quote: His design was to visit India, in the belief that he had in his knowledge of its various languages, and in the views he had taken of its society, the means of materially assisting the progress of European colonization and trade.

entries.what: Victor and Clerval travel through Windsor, Oxford, Matlock, and the Cumberland lakes on their way north, planning to finish the tour by July.
entries.when: They quitted London on the 27th of March; they resolve to arrive at the completion of this tour about the end of July.
entries.why: They received a letter from a Scotch friend in Scotland asking if the beauties of his native country were sufficient allurements to prolong their journey to Perth.
entries.quote: We accordingly determined to commence our journey towards the north at the expiration of another month. In this expedition we did not intend to follow the great road to Edinburgh, but to visit Windsor, Oxford, Matlock, and the Cumberland lakes, resolving to arrive at the completion of this tour about the end of July.

entries.what: Victor enjoys Oxford's historical sites but feels his enjoyment is embittered by memories of the past and anticipation of the future.
entries.when: After passing some months in London, they travel to Oxford; they stay a considerable period there.
entries.why: The memory of Charles I and his companions, and the fate of Hampden, elevate his soul momentarily but then depress him again.
entries.quote: If these feelings had not found an imaginary gratification, the appearance of the city had yet in itself sufficient beauty to obtain our admiration.

entries.what: Victor and Clerval visit Matlock, where the scenery resembles Switzerland but on a lower scale, and the name Chamounix makes Victor tremble.
entries.when: From Oxford they proceeded to Matlock; they later spend two months in Cumberland and Westmorland.
entries.why: The country near Matlock resembles Switzerland; the name Chamounix is associated with a terrible scene for Victor.
entries.quote: The latter name made me tremble when pronounced by Henry, and I hastened to quit Matlock, with which that terrible scene was thus associated.

entries.what: Victor feels a connection to the Cumberland and Westmorland mountains, resembling the Swiss mountains of his native country.
entries.when: From Derby, they passed two months in Cumberland and Westmorland.
entries.why: The little patches of snow on northern mountain sides, lakes, and rocky streams were familiar and dear sights to Victor.
entries.quote: I could now almost fancy myself among the Swiss mountains. The little patches of snow which yet lingered on the northern sides of the mountains, the lakes, and the dashing of the rocky streams were all familiar and dear sights to me.

entries.what: Victor is tormented by fear that the monster will kill Clerval if he is absent, and he follows Clerval closely to protect him.
entries.when: During their journey north, especially when letters from Elizabeth or his father are delayed or arrive.
entries.why: Victor fears the monster followed him and might expedite his remissness by murdering his companion; he feels guilty drawing a curse upon his head.
entries.quote: Sometimes I thought that the fiend followed me and might expedite my remissness by murdering my companion. When these thoughts possessed me, I would not quit Henry for a moment, but followed him as his shadow, to protect him from the fancied rage of his destroyer.

entries.what: Victor travels alone to the Orkneys to finish his work in solitude, fearing the monster's discovery.
entries.when: Having parted from Clerval at Perth, he traversed the northern highlands and fixed on one of the remotest of the Orkneys.
entries.why: He did not doubt the monster followed him and would discover himself when he had finished, that he might receive his companion.
entries.quote: I determined to visit some remote spot of Scotland and finish my work in solitude. I did not doubt but that the monster followed me and would discover himself to me when I should have finished, that he might receive his companion.

entries.what: Victor settles in a wretched hut on a remote Orkney island, working by day and walking the beach by night to listen to the waves.
entries.when: After arriving at the Orkneys, he devotes mornings to labour and evenings to walking on the stony beach.
entries.why: The island is fitted for such work, hardly more than a rock beaten by waves; the hut is miserable with barren soil and squalor.
entries.quote: On the whole island there were but three miserable huts, and one of these was vacant when I arrived. This I hired. It contained but two rooms, and these exhibited all the squalidness of the most miserable penury.

entries.what: Victor's labour becomes increasingly horrible and irksome; he works coldly and his heart sickens at his work.
entries.when: As he proceeded in his labour in the Orkneys, it became every day more horrible and irksome.
entries.why: He went to it in cold blood, unlike his first experiment where enthusiastic frenzy blinded him to the horror.
entries.quote: But now I went to it in cold blood, and my heart often sickened at the work of my hands.

entries.what: Victor sits in his laboratory one evening, reflecting on whether to continue his work, and sees the monster at the casement.
entries.quote: I sat one evening in my laboratory; the sun had set, and the moon was just rising from the sea

entries.what: The monster demands Victor create a female companion, threatening vengeance if he refuses.
entries.quote: You have destroyed the work which you began; what is it that you intend? Do you dare to break your promise?

entries.what: Victor destroys the half-finished female creature in a fit of moral revulsion.
entries.when: Chapter 20, after the monster's plea and Victor's resolve
entries.quote: trembling with passion, tore to pieces the thing on which I was engaged

entries.what: Victor flees the island by boat, throws the remains of his work into the sea, and is driven far from shore by a storm.
entries.when: Chapter 20, night after the laboratory confrontation
entries.quote: I then, putting my basket aboard a little skiff, sailed out about four miles from the shore

entries.what: The magistrate and witnesses examine Victor after his arrest, during which he recognizes the finger marks on the dead body as those of his brother William's murderer, causing extreme agitation.
entries.why: The deposition describes a body found with black finger marks on the neck, which triggers Victor's memory of William's murder.
entries.quote: when the mark of the fingers was mentioned I remembered the murder of my brother and felt myself extremely agitated; my limbs trembled, and a mist came over my eyes

entries.what: Daniel Nugent testifies he saw a boat with a single man near the shore just before the body was discovered, matching the boat Victor arrived in.
entries.why: Daniel Nugent's testimony places a boat with one man near the shore at the time of the discovery, linking Victor to the crime scene.
entries.quote: he saw a boat, with a single man in it, at a short distance from the shore; and as far as he could judge by the light of a few stars, it was the same boat in which I had just landed

entries.what: A woman living near the beach saw a boat with one man push off from the shore where the body was later found, about an hour before the fishermen discovered it.
entries.why: This sighting places a single-man boat departing from the exact location where the corpse was discovered.
entries.quote: she saw a boat with only one man in it push off from that part of the shore where the corpse was afterwards found

entries.what: The body found on the shore is identified as Henry Clerval, Victor's friend, who was strangled with finger marks on his neck.
entries.why: The body is described as a handsome young man about 25 years old with black finger marks on the neck, no sign of violence except the strangulation.
entries.quote: He had apparently been strangled, for there was no sign of any violence except the black mark of fingers on his neck.

entries.what: Victor is brought into the room where Henry Clerval's body lies and immediately recognizes him, crying out in horror and agony.
entries.why: Victor sees the lifeless form of Henry Clerval and is overcome with the belief that his own creation has destroyed his friend.
entries.quote: the lifeless form of Henry Clerval stretched before me. I gasped for breath, and throwing myself on the body, I exclaimed, 'Have my murderous machinations deprived you also, my dearest Henry, of life?'

entries.what: Victor falls into a feverish illness lasting two months, during which he raves about being the murderer of William, Justine, and Clerval, and sometimes feels the monster's grasp on his neck.
entries.why: The sight of Clerval's body triggers a nervous collapse; Victor raves and is attended by a physician and nurse.
entries.quote: I lay for two months on the point of death; my ravings, as I afterwards heard, were frightful; I called myself the murderer of William, of Justine, and of Clerval. Sometimes I felt the fingers of the monster already grasping my neck

entries.what: Mr. Kirwin examines Victor's papers, including a letter from Victor's father, and writes to Geneva reporting Victor's illness and imprisonment.
entries.why: Mr. Kirwin wanted to send word to Victor's relations about his misfortune and illness, so he reviewed the papers on Victor's person.
entries.quote: Immediately upon your being taken ill, all the papers that were on your person were brought me, and I examined them that I might discover some trace by which I could send to your relations an account of your misfortune and illness.

entries.what: Mr. Kirwin tells Victor that his family is well and that a friend has come to visit him, which causes Victor to fear the murderer has come to taunt him.
entries.why: Mr. Kirwin informs Victor of his family's status and a visitor's arrival, prompting Victor's anguished reaction.
entries.quote: I know that the sympathy of a stranger can be but of little relief to one borne down as you are by so strange a misfortune. But you will, I hope, soon quit this melancholy abode, for doubtless evidence can easily be brought to free you from the criminal charge.

entries.what: Victor's father arrives at the prison, bringing Victor great joy, and they discuss the welfare of the family, including Elizabeth and Ernest.
entries.why: Victor's father comes to visit him in prison, calming Victor with assurances of his family's safety.
entries.quote: My father entered it. Nothing, at this moment, could have given me greater pleasure than the arrival of my father. I stretched out my hand to him and cried, 'Are you, then, safe--and Elizabeth--and Ernest?'

entries.what: The grand jury rejects the criminal charge against Victor because evidence proves he was on the Orkney Islands when the body was found, leading to his release.
entries.why: The grand jury rejected the bill after it was proved Victor was on the Orkney Islands at the hour the body of his friend was found.
entries.quote: the grand jury rejected the bill, on its being proved that I was on the Orkney Islands at the hour the body of my friend was found

entries.what: Victor is released from prison and sails for Havre-de-Grace with his father, looking toward Geneva while tormented by memories of Clerval and the monster.
entries.why: After his release, Victor travels toward Geneva with his father, still haunted by the deaths of his friends and the monster's presence.
entries.quote: We took our passage on board a vessel bound for Havre-de-Grace and sailed with a fair wind from the Irish shores. It was midnight. I lay on the deck looking at the stars and listening to the dashing of the waves.

entries.what: The voyage ends and Victor and his father travel to Paris, where Victor falls ill and must rest before continuing.
entries.quote: The voyage came to an end. We landed, and proceeded to Paris.

entries.what: Victor feels intense guilt and isolation, believing he has no right to mingle with humanity because he created a murderous daemon.
entries.quote: I had unchained an enemy among them whose joy it was to shed their blood and to revel in their groans.

entries.what: Victor confesses to his father that he murdered William, Justine, and Henry, believing he is the cause of their deaths.
entries.quote: Justine, poor unhappy Justine, was as innocent as I, and she suffered the same charge; she died for it; and I am the cause of this--I murdered her. William, Justine, and Henry--they all died by my hands.

entries.what: Victor's father dismisses his confession as delirium or imagination, not believing Victor's claims of guilt.
entries.quote: when I thus accused myself, he sometimes seemed to desire an explanation, and at others he appeared to consider it as the offspring of delirium.

entries.what: Elizabeth writes a letter to Victor expressing her love and asking if he loves another, fearing he may regret their engagement.
entries.quote: Do you not love another? You have travelled; you have spent several years of your life at Ingolstadt...

entries.what: Victor resolves not to delay his marriage to Elizabeth, fearing the daemon's threat on his wedding night will harm her if he postpones.
entries.quote: I resolved, therefore, that if my immediate union with my cousin would conduce either to hers or my father's happiness, my adversary's designs against my life should not retard it a single hour.

entries.what: Victor and Elizabeth travel to Geneva after their marriage preparations, stopping at Evian for the night before continuing their journey.
entries.quote: After the ceremony was performed a large party assembled at my father's, but it was agreed that Elizabeth and I should commence our journey by water, sleeping that night at Evian and continuing our voyage on the following day.

entries.what: Victor and Elizabeth enjoy a seemingly happy day on the lake, but the mood turns melancholy as they approach their destination, foreshadowing doom.
entries.quote: The sun sank beneath the horizon as we landed, and as I touched the shore I felt those cares and fears revive which soon were to clasp me and cling to me forever.

entries.what: Victor and Elizabeth land at 8 PM and walk on the shore before retiring to an inn.
entries.quote: It was eight o'clock when we landed; we walked for a short time on the shore

entries.what: A heavy storm of rain descends suddenly during the night.
entries.quote: Suddenly a heavy storm of rain descended.

entries.what: Victor is terrified and armed with a pistol, fearing an encounter with his creation.
entries.quote: I was anxious and watchful, while my right hand grasped a pistol which was hidden in my bosom; every sound terrified me

entries.what: Elizabeth asks Victor what he fears after seeing his terrified glance.
entries.quote: What is it that agitates you, my dear Victor? What is it you fear?

entries.what: Victor urges Elizabeth to retire to another room, fearing for her safety.
entries.quote: I earnestly entreated her to retire, resolving not to join her until I had obtained some knowledge as to the situation of my enemy.

entries.what: A shrill scream comes from the room where Elizabeth has retired.
entries.quote: suddenly I heard a shrill and dreadful scream. It came from the room into which Elizabeth had retired.

entries.what: Victor finds Elizabeth dead on the bed with the monster's finger marks on her neck.
entries.quote: She was there, lifeless and inanimate, thrown across the bed, her head hanging down and her pale and distorted features half covered by her hair. Everywhere I turn I see the same figure--her bloodless arms and relaxed form flung by the murderer on its bridal bier.

entries.what: The monster appears at the window and jeers at Victor over Elizabeth's corpse.
entries.quote: I saw at the open window a figure the most hideous and abhorred. A grin was on the face of the monster; he seemed to jeer, as with his fiendish finger he pointed towards the corpse of my wife.

entries.what: Victor fires a pistol at the monster, who escapes into the lake.
entries.quote: I rushed towards the window, and drawing a pistol from my bosom, fired; but he eluded me, leaped from his station, and running with the swiftness of lightning, plunged into the lake.

entries.what: Victor searches in vain for the monster by boat and net, then returns home in exhaustion.
entries.quote: After passing several hours, we returned hopeless... After having landed, they proceeded to search the country... I fell at last in a state of utter exhaustion.

entries.what: Victor sees the monster's reflection in the moonlit chamber and realizes the truth of his creation's vengeance.
entries.quote: The windows of the room had before been darkened, and I felt a kind of panic on seeing the pale yellow light of the moon illuminate the chamber. The shutters had been thrown back, and with a sensation of horror not to be described, I saw at the open window a figure the most hideous and abhorred.

entries.what: Victor's father dies of grief after learning of Elizabeth's death.
entries.why: the former sunk under the tidings that I bore... the springs of existence suddenly gave way; he was unable to rise from his bed, and in a few days he died in my arms.
entries.quote: My father even now might be writhing under his grasp, and Ernest might be dead at his feet. This idea made me shudder and recalled me to action. I started up and resolved to return to Geneva with all possible speed... My father excellent and venerable old man! His eyes wandered in vacancy... he died in my arms.

entries.what: Victor is imprisoned as mad and later seeks revenge on the monster.
entries.quote: They had called me mad, and during many months, as I understood, a solitary cell had been my habitation. Liberty, however, had been a useless gift to me, had I not, as I awakened to reason, at the same time awakened to revenge.

entries.what: Victor tells a magistrate about the monster and demands his capture.
entries.when: about a month after my release
entries.quote: I repaired to a criminal judge in the town and told him that I had an accusation to make, that I knew the destroyer of my family, and that I required him to exert his whole authority for the apprehension of the murderer.

entries.what: The magistrate doubts Victor's story and refuses to pursue the monster due to his supernatural abilities.
entries.quote: the creature of whom you speak appears to have powers which would put all my exertions to defiance. Who can follow an animal which can traverse the sea of ice and inhabit caves and dens where no man would venture to intrude?

entries.what: Victor Frankenstein leaves Geneva forever, taking money and his mother's jewels, driven by a desire for revenge against his creation.
entries.why: His country became hateful to him in his adversity, and he was driven by fury and revenge.
entries.quote: My first resolution was to quit Geneva forever; my country, which, when I was happy and beloved, was dear to me, now, in my adversity, became hateful.

entries.what: Victor swears an oath on the sacred earth and the spirits of the night to pursue the daemon until one of them perishes.
entries.when: Chapter 24, during the night after William's grave
entries.why: He feels eternal grief and wants to destroy the daemon who caused the deaths of his loved ones.
entries.quote: By the sacred earth on which I kneel, by the shades that wander near me, by the deep and eternal grief that I feel, I swear; and by thee, O Night, and the spirits that preside over thee, to pursue the daemon who caused this misery, until he or I shall perish in mortal conflict.

entries.what: A fiendish laughter and a voice address Victor, telling him he is satisfied that Victor has determined to live for vengeance.
entries.when: Chapter 24, night after Victor's oath at the cemetery
entries.why: The daemon appears to acknowledge Victor's vow and mocks him from nearby.
entries.quote: I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have determined to live, and I am satisfied.

entries.what: Victor pursues the daemon across Europe, following the Rhone River and crossing the Mediterranean to the Black Sea.
entries.why: He seeks a clue to trace the daemon's steps and continues his pilgrimage of revenge.
entries.quote: I followed the windings of the Rhone, but vainly. The blue Mediterranean appeared, and by a strange chance, I saw the fiend enter by night and hide himself in a vessel bound for the Black Sea.

entries.what: Victor endures extreme hardships during his pursuit, including cold, famine, and exhaustion, but is sustained by hope and occasional providential aid.
entries.when: Chapter 24, during his travels through Tartary and Russia
entries.why: He is cursed by a devil and carries an eternal hell within him, yet good spirits guide his steps and provide food and warmth.
entries.quote: Cold, want, and fatigue were the least pains which I was destined to endure; I was cursed by some devil and carried about with me my eternal hell; yet still a spirit of good followed and directed my steps.

entries.what: The daemon leaves inscriptions on trees and stones, goading Victor to follow him toward the 'everlasting ices of the north'.
entries.why: The daemon wants to lead Victor into a journey where his sufferings will satisfy the daemon's everlasting hatred.
entries.quote: My reign is not yet over--these words were legible in one of these inscriptions--'you live, and my power is complete. Follow me; I seek the everlasting ices of the north.'

entries.what: Victor travels across the frozen ocean on a sledge, gaining ground on the daemon until a fissure in the ice separates them.
entries.when: Chapter 24, journey toward the north pole
entries.why: The daemon had fled across the sea, and Victor pursues him onto the frozen ocean, gaining until they are a mile apart.
entries.quote: When, after nearly two days' journey, I beheld my enemy at no more than a mile distant, my heart bounded within me.

entries.what: A massive crack in the ice creates a sea between Victor and the daemon, leaving Victor on a shrinking ice raft as his dogs die.
entries.when: Chapter 24, near the end of the pursuit
entries.why: The sea splits open, overwhelming Victor and separating him from the daemon, who escapes onto open water.
entries.quote: In a few minutes a tumultuous sea rolled between me and my enemy, and I was left drifting on a scattered piece of ice that was continually lessening.

entries.what: Victor is rescued by Robert Walton's ship and begs Walton to kill the daemon if Victor dies, fearing the daemon will survive and continue his crimes.
entries.why: Victor's task is unfulfilled, and he fears the daemon will live to add to his dark crimes; he begs Walton to swear vengeance.
entries.quote: If I do, swear to me, Walton, that he shall not escape, that you will seek him and satisfy my vengeance in his death.

entries.what: The creature believes that when dreaming he holds converse with his friends, who are not creations of fancy but beings from a remote world.
entries.quote: he believes that when in dreams he holds converse with his friends and derives from that communion consolation for his miseries or excitements to his vengeance, that they are not the creations of his fancy, but the beings themselves who visit him from the regions of a remote world.

entries.what: The creature feels his own worth and the greatness of his fall, reflecting on how glorious he must have been in days of prosperity.
entries.quote: What a glorious creature must he have been in the days of his prosperity, when he is thus noble and godlike in ruin!

entries.what: The creature believes his talents and ambition were once great, but now he is chained in an eternal hell like the archangel who aspired to omnipotence.
entries.quote: like the archangel who aspired to omnipotence, I am chained in an eternal hell.

entries.what: The creature states that no new ties or fresh affections can replace those who are gone, especially childhood companions like Clerval and Elizabeth.
entries.quote: Can any man be to me as Clerval was, or any woman another Elizabeth?  Even where the affections are not strongly moved by any superior excellence, the companions of our childhood always possess a certain power over our minds which hardly any later friend can obtain.

entries.what: The creature's only feeling that can persuade him to preserve his life is if he were engaged in a high undertaking or design fraught with extensive utility to fellow creatures.
entries.quote: If I were engaged in any high undertaking or design, fraught with extensive utility to my fellow creatures, then could I live to fulfil it.

entries.what: The creature is determined to pursue and destroy the being he gave existence to, as his destiny, after which he may die.
entries.quote: I must pursue and destroy the being to whom I gave existence; then my lot on earth will be fulfilled and I may die.

entries.what: The crew demands that Victor promise to direct the vessel southwards if freed from ice, fearing he would lead them into fresh dangers.
entries.why: The sailors feared Victor would be rash enough to continue the voyage and lead them into danger after overcoming the ice.
entries.quote: They insisted, therefore, that I should engage with a solemn promise that if the vessel should be freed I would instantly direct my course southwards.

entries.what: Frankenstein rebukes the sailors' fear of danger, declaring the expedition glorious because it is full of perils and terror, and urges them to be steady and firm as a rock.
entries.why: To inspire the sailors to endure the hardships and not turn back from the expedition due to fear.
entries.quote: Did you not call this a glorious expedition? And wherefore was it glorious? Not because the way was smooth and placid as a southern sea, but because it was full of dangers and terror...

entries.what: The ice begins to move and roar like thunder on September 9th, and on the 11th the passage towards the south becomes free.
entries.when: September 9th, the ice began to move... on the 11th the passage towards the south became perfectly free.
entries.quote: September 9th, the ice began to move, and roarings like thunder were heard at a distance as the islands split and cracked in every direction.

entries.what: The sailors shout with tumultuous joy upon seeing the passage free and their return to England assured, while Frankenstein refuses to turn back from his pursuit.
entries.why: The sailors' return to their native country was apparently assured, but Frankenstein insists on continuing his pursuit of the creature.
entries.quote: When the sailors saw this and that their return to their native country was apparently assured, a shout of tumultuous joy broke from them, loud and long-continued.

entries.what: Frankenstein consents to return to England if not destroyed, his hopes blasted by cowardice and indecision.
entries.why: He had consented to return if the vessel was not destroyed, feeling his purpose unfulfilled and fearing shame.
entries.quote: The die is cast; I have consented to return if we are not destroyed. Thus are my hopes blasted by cowardice and indecision;

entries.what: On September 12th, Frankenstein is returning to England, having lost his hopes of utility and glory and his friend.
entries.why: He is wafted towards England towards his sister, detailing bitter circumstances.
entries.quote: September 12th. It is past; I am returning to England. I have lost my hopes of utility and glory; I have lost my friend.

entries.what: Victor Frankenstein dies after a prolonged illness, speaking his final words to Walton about revenge and duty.
entries.why: Victor had been ill for a long time; the surgeon ordered him undisturbed, and he died after a brief rally.
entries.quote: At length he opened his eyes; he breathed with difficulty and was unable to speak. The surgeon gave him a composing draught and ordered us to leave him undisturbed.

entries.what: Victor urges Walton to seek happiness in tranquility and avoid ambition, especially in science.
entries.why: Victor reflects on his own blasting in hopes and warns Walton against similar fate.
entries.quote: Seek happiness in tranquillity and avoid ambition, even if it be only the apparently innocent one of distinguishing yourself in science and discoveries.

entries.what: The Creature vows to kill himself on a funeral pyre after Victor's death.
entries.why: The Creature declares his work is nearly complete and he will seek the most northern extremity to consume himself.
entries.quote: I shall quit your vessel on the ice raft which brought me thither and shall seek the most northern extremity of the globe; I shall collect my funeral pile and consume to ashes this miserable frame.

entries.what: The Creature expresses remorse and self-loathing, calling himself a wretch and an abortion.
entries.why: The Creature reflects on his crimes, including the murder of Clerval and the pursuit of Victor to ruin.
entries.quote: I look on the hands which executed the deed; I think on the heart in which the imagination of it was conceived and long for the moment when these hands will meet my eyes.

entries.what: The Creature declares his work of vengeance is complete with Victor's death.
entries.why: The Creature states that his last victim is Victor and that his series of being is wound to its close.
entries.quote: In his murder my crimes are consummated; the miserable series of my being is wound to its close!

entries.what: The Creature vows to disappear into the northern wilderness and die, taking his remembrance of Victor with him.
entries.why: The Creature resolves to collect his funeral pile and be consumed by fire so that no curious wretch can create another like him.
entries.quote: I shall no longer see the sun or stars or feel the winds play on my cheeks. Light, feeling, and sense will pass away; and in this condition must I find my happiness.

entries.what: The Creature leaps from the cabin window onto an ice raft and is borne away by waves into darkness.
entries.why: The Creature exits the narrative to fulfill his vow of self-destruction in the northern wilderness.
entries.quote: He sprang from the cabin window as he said this, upon the ice raft which lay close to the vessel. He was soon borne away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance.
